title: Modeling Disease Transmission via Fluid Dynamics
abstract: Air, water, and human body fluids are the primary infection vectors for the transmission of most infectious diseases. Fluid dynamics, which offers the tools to study how viruses are carried and dispersed throughout different environments, is required to learn about this process. This chapter is dedicated to modeling basic infectious disease model where the transmission medium can be airborne, waterborne, and contact-based through utilization of fundamental principles of fluid dynamic principles, such as the Navier-Stokes equations and particle transport theory. Within the context of epidemiological modeling, scientists can forecast infectious particle movement within complex spaces using computational fluid dynamics (CFD), which can take into consideration surface interactions, humidity, and airflow. CFD, upon application, it models the process of infection in a manner analogous to the movement of fluid, leading to a more accurate representation of disease spread. The model is solved numerically with a non-standard finite difference (NSFD) scheme that retains essential features of the biological system while maintaining numerical stability. Using a numerical example, this strategy is demonstrated through simulations, revealing infection spread at various times within a two-dimensional special region. The importance of CFD models in predicting the spread of infectious diseases is presented through case studies, such as the spread of COVID-19, influenza, measles and cholera. These case studies illustrate how fluid mechanics and epidemiology studies can be combined to provide informative input for public health planning and infection control. Finally, our modeling framework is a useful instrument for projecting the transmission risks and helping determine preventive actions in indoor and outdoor settings.

title_original: What the West Texas Measles Outbreak Taught Me About Public Health Leadership

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to examine the lessons learned from the West Texas measles outbreak regarding public health leadership and response strategies.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a commentary on the West Texas measles outbreak, which occurred in 2026, and focuses on public health leadership and management practices during the event.
analysis.methods: The methods involved a retrospective analysis of public health leadership strategies and outcomes during the West Texas measles outbreak, including case management, communication protocols, and community engagement.
analysis.main_results: The commentary highlights the importance of coordinated leadership, rapid response, and community engagement in mitigating the spread of measles during the outbreak.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the outbreak as a case study demonstrating the critical role of effective public health leadership in managing infectious disease outbreaks, offering novel insights into leadership practices.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform public health leadership training and preparedness for future outbreaks, emphasizing the need for proactive and collaborative strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a commentary and does not include quantitative data, which limits the strength of the evidence but provides valuable qualitative insights.

analysis.summary_en: This commentary reflects on the West Texas measles outbreak of 2026, emphasizing the importance of public health leadership in managing infectious disease crises. The study outlines the challenges faced during the outbreak and highlights the need for coordinated, rapid, and community-focused responses. While the analysis is qualitative and lacks quantitative data, it offers novel insights into leadership practices that can inform future outbreak management. The findings suggest that effective leadership is crucial for controlling measles outbreaks and improving public health preparedness. The study's limitations include its reliance on a narrative rather than empirical data, which affects the strength of the evidence but does not diminish its value as a case study.

Volume 32, Number 11—November 2026 Synopsis Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis after Measles Outbreaks, the Philippines, 2007–2022 Suggested citation for this article Abstract Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a delayed, almost uniformly fatal complication of measles. The Philippines had measles outbreaks in 2010–2011, 2013, and 2018–2019; the last was the largest in the World Health Organization Western Pacific Region. Published SSPE data from the Philippines end in 2015. We reviewed all 20 children admitted with SSPE to a tertiary pediatric hospital in Quezon City during 2007–2022 and estimated year of measles infection. Median patient age was 6.2 years at hospital admission and 0.7 years at reported measles illness. Five (25.0%) of 20 admissions occurred in 2022, and estimated infection dates placed 4 patients within the 2018–2019 outbreak; all were admitted during 2020–2022. Given the multiyear latency of SSPE, additional cases might emerge over coming years. Reported measles history could not be established in one quarter of patients. Strengthened measles surveillance and sustained 2-dose vaccination coverage are needed. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by persistent central nervous system infection with a defective, hypermutant measles virus. It typically follows measles acquired in early childhood after a latency of years and is almost always fatal (1,2). Because SSPE follows measles by years rather than weeks, the neurologic consequences of an outbreak do not become visible until long after the outbreak has ended. Measles vaccination was introduced in the Philippines in 1983; the first routine dose is scheduled at 9 months of age (3). Nationwide immunization campaigns in 1998 and 2004 were followed by historically low measles incidence in 2006 (3). First-dose measles-containing vaccine coverage later declined from 92% in 2004–2007 to 80% in 2015–2016 and 64% in 2021 (4). Reported measles cases rose sharply during a 2018–2019 outbreak, from 2,428 in 2017 to 48,525 in 2019, the largest outbreak in the World Health Organization Western Pacific Region during that period (5). Published data on SSPE in the Philippines are limited; the largest local series described children seen at a single tertiary hospital during 2005–2015 (6). No published series from the Philippines spans the period during which children infected in the 2018–2019 outbreak would be expected to demonstrate symptoms of SSPE. We describe children admitted with SSPE to a tertiary government pediatric hospital over 16 years and examine the distribution of their estimated years of measles infection against the national outbreak record. Design and Setting We retrospectively reviewed the records of all children admitted to National Children’s Hospital, a tertiary government pediatric hospital in Quezon City, the Philippines, with a final diagnosis of SSPE during January 1, 2007–December 31, 2022. All such patients were enumerated. The 2007 start date reflects the period from which complete institutional records and corresponding registry data were available. Case Definition We modified the case definition from Dyken’s criteria (1). We defined a case as a clinical diagnosis of SSPE by the attending pediatric neurologist on the basis of progressive neurologic deterioration with qualitatively positive measles antibody in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), serum, or both. We excluded children with bacterial, tuberculous, or viral meningitis and children with intracranial masses. Because quantitative measles antibody titers, CSF globulin fractionation, brain biopsy, and uniform electroencephalography were unavailable, we could not apply the full Dyken criteria; we classified cases as clinically diagnosed SSPE with varying levels of supportive evidence. Variables Age at reported measles infection and reported measles history came from parental or guardian recall recorded at admission; measles history was recorded as reported, absent, or unknown. Vaccination status was likewise based on parent or guardian report recorded at admission and was not consistently verified against immunization records. Estimation of Year of Reported Measles Infection For each patient, we calculated the interval between measles infection and development of SSPE as age at hospital admission minus age at measles infection. We obtained the estimated calendar year of measles infection by subtracting that interval from the year of admission. We then compared estimated infection years with the recorded periods of national measles outbreak activity. For the 14 children with a parent- or guardian-reported history of measles, we calculated the interval between reported measles illness and hospital admission. We excluded 3 children with a reported measles-to-admission interval of <1 year from the interval analysis, because such a short interval is atypical for SSPE and the timing of the reported measles illness could not be independently verified. A very short interval can also reflect acute measles encephalitis (within 14 days of rash onset) or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (within weeks), rather than SSPE, which follows a latency of years (1). Statistical Analysis We summarized categorical variables as frequencies and percentages and summarized continuous variables as medians with interquartile ranges. We did not group patients by admission year for comparison, because the multiyear interval between infection and admission makes such grouping uninterpretable. Analyses used Stata 16.1 (StataCorps LLC, https://www.stata.com) and Microsoft Excel (https://www.microsoft.com). The protocol was approved by the National Children’s Hospital Institutional Review Board (approval no. NCH-IRB 2023–12-NCT) using unlinked, deidentified data. Twenty children admitted during January 1, 2007–December 31, 2022, met the case definition. Cases were unevenly distributed across the study period (Figure, panel A). Eight (40.0%) of the 20 admissions occurred in the final 3 years of the series, and 5 (25.0%) admissions occurred in 2022 alone. Four patients had an estimated measles infection year of 2018 or 2019, corresponding to the national outbreak period (Figure, panel B); all 4 had a reported measles history and positive CSF antibody, and all were admitted during 2020–2022 with intervals of 2.1–3.5 years since measles infection. For 3 patients, the estimated infection year was 2004; estimated infection year for 1 patient was 2013. Most patients with an estimable year (14 of 19) were infected outside recognized outbreak periods, consistent with continued transmission between outbreaks. SSPE was suspected at time of admission in 9 (45.0%) patients. The remainder were admitted under other working diagnoses: probable intracranial mass in 4 (20.0%) patients, meningitis in 3 (15.0%) patients, encephalitis in 2 (10.0%) patients, and 1 (5.0%) each of acute rheumatic fever and traumatic brain injury. At discharge, 18 (90.0%) patients carried a diagnosis of SSPE and 2 (10.0%) patients probable SSPE. Of the 20 patients, 14 (70.0%) patients were male and 6 (30.0%) were female. The median age was 6.2 years at admission and 0.7 years at reported measles illness; 10 of the 19 patients with an estimable age were infected before the age of 9 months. Eight children had stunting or wasting, and 3 had comorbidities. A reported measles history was present in 15 (75.0%), unknown in 4 (20.0%), and absent in 1 (5.0%). Seventeen (85.0%) patients had received >1 measles-containing vaccine; 11 (55.0%) patients had received a single dose only. Twelve (60.0%) patients were admitted in stage 2 and 5 (25.0%) were admitted in stage 3 (Table; Appendix Table). Among the 14 children with a reported measles history, the median interval from measles to hospital admission was 5.8 (interquartile range 3.5–8.9) years. Among the 20 children, 5 had progressive neurologic deterioration, tested positive for measles antibody in CSF, and had characteristic electroencephalography; 12 had progressive deterioration and antibody-positive CSF without electroencephalography; and 3 had progressive deterioration with antibody-positive serum only. Measles antibody testing of CSF was performed in 17 patients and was positive in all 17; serum antibody was tested in 13 and positive in all 13. Both were tested in 10 patients; 3 patients had serum testing alone. Electroencephalography was performed in 5 patients (25.0%); all showed patterns consistent with SSPE (7). In this 16-year series, cases of SSPE clustered in recent years: 40% of admissions occurred in the last 3 years of the study period (2020–2022) and one quarter occurred in 2022 alone; 4 children had an estimated measles infection during the 2018–2019 outbreak. Because SSPE follows measles after a latency of years, those observations most likely represent the leading edge of a postoutbreak wave; additional cases might emerge over the coming years. For public health, the priority is heightened measles surveillance, early recognition of SSPE in children infected during recent outbreaks, and restoration of high 2-dose vaccination coverage. The short intervals between measles infection and SSPE (2.1–3.5 years) seen in the 4 outbreak-associated cases do not indicate shortening latency: a child infected in 2018 cannot show an interval beyond 4 years in a series closing in 2022, so recent cases are truncated by the observation window. First-dose coverage fell to 64% by 2021, enlarging the susceptible pool beyond the 2018–2019 cohort. A comparable postoutbreak resurgence of SSPE has been reported from the United Kingdom (8). A reported measles history was absent or unknown in a quarter of children; in those children, diagnosis rested on progressive neurodegeneration and presence of measles antibody in CSF or serum. Absence of a reported measles history is often used to argue against SSPE, yet such reasoning would have delayed or missed diagnosis in 5 of those 20 children. Measles antibody testing of CSF is therefore warranted in any child with progressive neurodegeneration and myoclonus, regardless of reported history. Although 85% of children had received a measles-containing vaccine, that does not implicate vaccination: SSPE follows wild-type measles, not the vaccine (1,2). Ten of 19 patients were infected before 9 months, the age of the first scheduled measles-containing vaccine dose in the Philippines (3) and an age group at particularly high risk for SSPE (1,2), and most had received only 1 dose. Those findings support earlier and more complete 2-dose coverage and supplementary immunization during outbreaks. The profile (male predominance, diagnostic delay of weeks to months) was broadly comparable with an earlier Philippines series (6); undernutrition and social disadvantage, noted locally (9), might limit timely vaccination and thereby raise measles and SSPE risk. SSPE cases in the Philippines currently cannot be staged against international criteria because quantitative antibody titers, CSF globulin fractionation, and consistent electroencephalography and neuroimaging are unavailable, a diagnostic-capacity gap worth closing in a country with recurrent measles outbreaks. The first limitation of this study is that, as a single-center retrospective review of 20 patients, it might not represent SSPE nationally, and no population denominator was available, so counts cannot be expressed as rates. Second, measles history, age at infection, and vaccination status were based on guardian recall and could not be verified; the infection-to-SSPE interval is therefore estimated and could not be determined in one quarter of children. Measles antibody was reported only qualitatively, and 3 children were diagnosed using serum antibody without CSF confirmation, although the temporal findings were unchanged when restricted to the 17 with CSF confirmation. Finally, molecular confirmation and genotyping, which require tissue, were not performed, and outcome after discharge was not available. In conclusion, measles antibody testing of CSF should be considered in any child with progressive neurodegeneration and myoclonus, irrespective of the reported measles history. Additional SSPE cases temporally associated with the 2018–2019 outbreak might continue to occur over the remainder of the 2020s. National surveillance for SSPE should be strengthened accordingly. Laboratory capacity should be developed for quantitative measles antibody titration in serum and CSF and for CSF globulin fractionation, so that Philippine cases can be characterized against international diagnostic criteria. Prospective studies capturing outcome and survival in children from the Philippines with SSPE are needed, as is evaluation of supportive and disease-modifying treatment in this population, building on the limited local experience with intravenous immunoglobulin (10). Efforts to restore and sustain 2-dose measles vaccination coverage, including supplementary immunization activities during outbreaks, remain the only means of preventing disease. Where postmortem or biopsy tissue is available, molecular confirmation of measles RNA and genotyping to link cases to circulating strains would strengthen future SSPE surveillance. Dr. Palisoc is a pediatric neurologist in the Section of Pediatric Neurology, National Children’s Hospital, Quezon City, and Associate Professor II at the Neuroscience Department, College of Medicine, San Beda University, Manila. Her research interests include pediatric epilepsy, neuroinfectious disease, and medical education. Acknowledgments We thank Tereynz Paul D. Mendoza for statistical analysis. M.P.P. conceived the study, designed and performed the analysis, and drafted the manuscript. M.S.R. acquired the data and verified the references and source data. R.D.G.J. reviewed the manuscript critically for important intellectual content. All authors approved the final version and agree to be accountable for all aspects of the work. The authors used Claude (Anthropic, https://www.anthropic.com) in preparing this manuscript. The tool assisted with verification of statistical calculations from data extracted by the authors, generation of the figure, and drafting and revision of the manuscript text. All source data were collected by the authors. All analyses were checked against the source data, all references were verified by the authors against the statements they support, and all content was reviewed and approved by the authors, who take full responsibility for the accuracy and integrity of the work. Design and Setting We retrospectively reviewed the records of all children admitted to National Children’s Hospital, a tertiary government pediatric hospital in Quezon City, the Philippines, with a final diagnosis of SSPE during January 1, 2007–December 31, 2022. All such patients were enumerated. The 2007 start date reflects the period from which complete institutional records and corresponding registry data were available. Case Definition We modified the case definition from Dyken’s criteria (1). We defined a case as a clinical diagnosis of SSPE by the attending pediatric neurologist on the basis of progressive neurologic deterioration with qualitatively positive measles antibody in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), serum, or both. We excluded children with bacterial, tuberculous, or viral meningitis and children with intracranial masses. Because quantitative measles antibody titers, CSF globulin fractionation, brain biopsy, and uniform electroencephalography were unavailable, we could not apply the full Dyken criteria; we classified cases as clinically diagnosed SSPE with varying levels of supportive evidence. Variables Age at reported measles infection and reported measles history came from parental or guardian recall recorded at admission; measles history was recorded as reported, absent, or unknown. Vaccination status was likewise based on parent or guardian report recorded at admission and was not consistently verified against immunization records. Estimation of Year of Reported Measles Infection For each patient, we calculated the interval between measles infection and development of SSPE as age at hospital admission minus age at measles infection. We obtained the estimated calendar year of measles infection by subtracting that interval from the year of admission. We then compared estimated infection years with the recorded periods of national measles outbreak activity. For the 14 children with a parent- or guardian-reported history of measles, we calculated the interval between reported measles illness and hospital admission. We excluded 3 children with a reported measles-to-admission interval of <1 year from the interval analysis, because such a short interval is atypical for SSPE and the timing of the reported measles illness could not be independently verified. A very short interval can also reflect acute measles encephalitis (within 14 days of rash onset) or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (within weeks), rather than SSPE, which follows a latency of years (1). title_original: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis after Measles Outbreaks, the Philippines, 2007–2022

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the association between measles outbreaks and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) in the Philippines from 2007 to 2022. The authors addressed the knowledge gap regarding the impact of measles outbreaks on SSPE cases, particularly in the context of declining vaccination coverage.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study retrospectively reviewed records of all children admitted to the National Children’s Hospital in Quezon City, Philippines, with a final diagnosis of SSPE from January 1, 2007, to December 31, 2022. The study included 20 patients, with 5 admissions in 2022, and estimated infection dates placed 4 patients within the 2018–2019 outbreak period.
analysis.methods: The study summarized categorical variables as frequencies and percentages and continuous variables as medians with interquartile ranges. Measles antibody testing was performed on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum samples, and electroencephalography (EEG) was conducted in 5 patients.
analysis.main_results: Of the 20 patients, 14 had an estimated measles infection year outside recognized outbreak periods, and 4 had a reported measles history and positive CSF antibody. The median age at reported measles infection was 0.7 years, and at hospital admission, it was 6.2 years. Measles antibody testing was positive in all 17 CSF samples and all 13 serum samples tested.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlighted that a reported measles history was absent or unknown in a quarter of children, emphasizing the importance of CSF antibody testing in diagnosing SSPE. The authors noted that 85% of children had received a measles-containing vaccine, but this does not implicate vaccination in SSPE, as it follows wild-type measles.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that continued measles transmission between outbreaks can lead to SSPE cases, even in vaccinated individuals. The study underscores the need for ongoing surveillance and vaccination efforts to prevent future outbreaks and SSPE cases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its single-center retrospective design, which may not represent SSPE nationally. Additionally, the absence of a population denominator means that counts cannot be expressed as rates. The study also notes that measles antibody was reported only qualitatively, and 3 children were diagnosed using serum antibody without CSF confirmation, although the temporal findings were unchanged when restricted to the 17 with CSF confirmation.

analysis.summary_en: This study retrospectively reviewed records of children with SSPE in the Philippines from 2007 to 2022, linking measles outbreaks to SSPE cases. It highlighted the importance of CSF antibody testing and the continued transmission of measles between outbreaks, even in vaccinated individuals.

analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 研究受到单中心回顾性设计的限制,可能无法代表全国范围内的SSPE情况。此外,缺乏人口分母意味着无法将计数表示为率。研究还指出,麻疹(麻疹)抗体仅定性报告,3名儿童仅通过血清抗体诊断而未进行CSF确认,尽管当仅限于17名CSF确认的患者时,时间发现没有变化。

title: Vaccination of patients with hematological malignancies: barriers and strategies to improve uptake

source_records.title: Vaccination of patients with hematological malignancies: barriers and strategies to improve uptake
Vaccination of patients with hematological malignancies: barriers and strategies to improve uptake

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: AbstractVaccination is one of the most successful developments in the history of medicine, having saved countless human lives. Although vaccination is of the utmost importance for patients with hematological neoplasms, it can also be challenging due to the often reduced or absent serological responses. Despite vaccination, breakthrough infections may occur among patients with hematological malignancies, particularly in those with impaired vaccine-induced immune responses. Although humoral responses are frequently impaired, vaccine-induced cellular immunity is preserved in a substantial proportion of patients with hematological malignancies and may contribute to protection against severe infections. Maximizing the immune response to vaccination requires optimal timing of vaccination relative to the administration of antineoplastic therapy. Patients may also fear vaccine side effects and worry that vaccination might influence their cancer therapy. Finally, some medical professionals, family members, and caregivers are insufficiently aware of the importance of vaccination for patients with hematological diseases, as well as their own vaccination. Despite significant developments in the field of vaccination of immunocompromised patients, addressing these challenges will require further high-quality clinical and translational research; continuous education of patients and healthcare providers; and enhanced cooperation and coordination among primary care practitioners, and epidemiological and hematological departments.Keywords: barriers, hematology, immunity, immunocompromised, vaccination 4.Breakthrough infection in vaccinated patients with hematological neoplasmsThe above-described results indicate that active infections occur after vaccination in many patients who are undergoing treatment for malignant hematological disease. However, there is a lack of data regarding breakthrough infections (with diseases other than COVID-19) in patients with hematological malignancies.Pagano et al. investigated 1,548 cases of breakthrough COVID-19 infections in adult patients with hematological malignancies, who had received at least one dose of an anti-SARS-CoV-2 vaccine between January 2021 and March 2022. They concluded that although mortality was significantly reduced compared to in the pre-vaccination era, breakthrough COVID-19 in this population was still associated with considerable mortality (42). Similarly, in a retrospective cohort analysis of almost 6,000 hematological patients, Mittelman et al. showed that vaccinated individuals with hematological neoplasms (particularly those undergoing active treatment) experience worse outcomes from breakthrough COVID-19 infections, compared to vaccinated individuals with an intact immune system (43).Wang et al. reported a 13.4% cumulative risk of breakthrough infection among patients with hematological malignancies, ranging from 11.0% in acute lymphocytic leukemia to 17.2% in multiple myeloma, and 17.4% in chronic myeloid leukemia, compared to a significantly lower 4.5% risk among controls. Moreover, hematological patients who experienced breakthrough infections exhibited a 37.8% overall risk of hospitalization, which was markedly higher than the 2.2% risk observed in those without breakthrough infections. Accordingly, the overall mortality risk was 5.7% in patients with breakthrough infections, compared to 0.8% in those without. Together, these findings indicate that, even among fully vaccinated individuals, the risk of breakthrough infections is significantly higher in patients with hematological tumors compared to those without cancer, and that such infections are associated with substantial clinical consequences, including increased rates of hospitalization and mortality (44).A prospective, multicenter, registry-based cohort study conducted in Spain included 1,394 patients with hematological disorders and reported that 37 (2.6%) developed breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection at a median of 77 days (range 7–195) after full vaccination. Most patients were asymptomatic (19/37, 51.4%), while 19% developed pneumonia, and the overall mortality rate was 8%. In multivariate logistic regression analysis, the absence of detectable antibodies at 3–6 weeks after complete vaccination emerged as the only factor associated with the occurrence of breakthrough infection (45).Piñana et al. also reported that 266 (17%) of 1,551 hematological patients developed breakthrough COVID-19 infection, occurring at a median of 86 days (range 7–391) after full vaccination. Multivariate analysis showed higher rates of breakthrough infection in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (29%) and in those receiving corticosteroids (24.5%), and lower incidence rates in female patients (15.5%) and in those whose last therapy was more than one year ago (14%). Median antibody titers at multiple time-points were significantly lower in patients with breakthrough infections, compared to those without. The cohort exhibited a low SARS-CoV-2-related mortality rate of 1.9% (46). 5.Response to vaccination in patients with hematological neoplasms, according to antineoplastic drugsIn their review, Fattizzo et al. have comprehensively summarized all recent data regarding the impact of different drugs on responses to COVID-19 vaccinations, and other vaccines in the era of targeted therapies (47). Many of the novel targeted therapies used for hematologic disease treatment can exert on-target or off-target immunomodulatory effects, which may influence responses to COVID-19 vaccines, and other vaccines. Agents that predominantly affect B cells—such as anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies, BTK inhibitors, and anti-CD19 CAR T cells—have the most pronounced negative impacts on seroconversion after vaccination, including with vaccines against COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcus, tetanus, and diphtheria toxoid (47). In contrast, JAK2 inhibitors, BCL-2 inhibitors, and hypomethylating agents may reduce immune function, but they appear to have less marked effects on the humoral response to vaccination (47). On the other hand, vaccine efficacy does not seem to be significantly compromised by tyrosine kinase inhibitors used to treat chronic myeloid leukemia and some anti-myeloma therapies, such as proteasome inhibitors and immunomodulatory agents (47). However, reduced seroconversion rates have been observed in patients treated with anti-CD38 and anti-BCMA monoclonal antibodies. Complement inhibitors used for complement-mediated hematologic disorders, and immunosuppressive therapies used for aplastic anemia, generally do not alter seroconversion rates; however, the overall magnitude of the immune response may be diminished in patients receiving steroids or anti-thymocyte globulin (47). 6.Effectiveness of booster doses in patients with hematological neoplasmsRecent studies of vaccination against COVID-19 have documented how booster doses impact the overall immune response after vaccination in immunocompromised patients with hematological tumors (Table 2). Huang et al. demonstrated that among 68 patients with hematologic neoplasms (including lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma, and acute and chronic myeloid leukemia), 89.7% achieved seroconversion following booster vaccination. Multivariate analysis revealed that effective neutralization was independently predicted by the absence of B-cell-targeted therapy within six months before vaccination, and higher immunoglobulin levels. The authors concluded that most patients with hematologic malignancies can achieve seroconversion after booster doses; however, ongoing B-cell depletion and hypogammaglobulinemia were negative predictive factors associated with poorer neutralizing responses (48).Table 2Effectiveness of COVID-19 booster doses in patients with hematological malignancies.Effectiveness of COVID-19 booster doses in patients with hematological malignanciesStudyPatient populationSeroconversion Huang et al. (48)Various hematological malignancies89.7% Shapiro et al. (49)Various hematological malignancies56% Šušol et al. (50)Various hematological malignancies23% Lim & Ahearne (51)B-cell NHL (No anti-CD20 in 12 months)92%B-cell NHL (anti-CD20 in 12 months)17%Table 3The main reasons for COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy among cancer patients (77).Reasons for COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy among cancer patients Doubts about the effectiveness of the vaccine Fear that the vaccine may interfere with and/or delay cancer treatment Vaccine safety concerns Beliefs regarding inadequate development of the vaccine Perception of low subjective risk regarding the diseaseShapiro and colleagues reported that administration of one booster vaccine dose increased the response rate to 56% in patients with hematological malignancies. Prior anti-CD20/BTK inhibitor therapy was associated with reduced vaccine efficacy (49). In another study, Šušol et al. reported that 23% (14/61) of patients with initial failure achieved seroconversion after the third dose, with the worst result in the group of patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (50). Finally, Lim and Ahearne showed that among patients with B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, the administration of a third vaccine dose led to improved humoral responses in 92% of those who had not received anti-CD20 therapy within the previous 12 months, compared to only 17% of those who had (51). Patients with indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma also exhibited enhanced humoral responses after the third dose; however, approximately one-third still exhibited relatively low antibody levels. It was concluded that although a third (booster) dose can partially improve immune responses, a substantial proportion of patients with NHL continue to show lower antibody levels compared with healthy individuals (51).Collectively, these findings indicate that booster vaccination can substantially enhance vaccine-induced humoral responses in a proportion of patients with hematological malignancies. The benefit is particularly limited in patients receiving B-cell-depleting or other B-cell-targeted therapies. 7.Benefits of vaccination for patients with malignant hematological neoplasmsThe numerous studies showing weaker immune responses to vaccination in hematological patients, even after administration of a booster dose (especially in some diseases and after certain therapies), raise questions regarding whether some patients with hematological malignancies benefit from vaccination at all. In a Cochrane systematic review, Cheuk et al. assessed the efficacy of viral vaccines in immunocompromised patients with hematological malignancies, including five randomized controlled trials evaluating inactivated influenza vaccines. This systematic review concluded that, despite attenuated serological responses, influenza vaccination was associated with reduced infection rates and fewer hospitalizations, supporting its routine administration in this high-risk population (52).Rossi et al. examined factors associated with mortality among hematological patients over 65 years old during the COVID-19 pandemic and found that both vaccination status and the number of vaccine doses received had significant impacts on 90-day survival (53). The 90-day survival probability progressively increased in patients who received zero, one, two, three, or four doses, with statistically significant differences observed across all pairwise group comparisons (53). Thus, the benefit of vaccination should not be assessed solely by antibody responses, but also by clinically meaningful outcomes, including prevention of infection where demonstrable, reduction in disease severity, hospitalization, and mortality among vaccinated compared with unvaccinated patients. Accordingly, the large EPICOVIDEHA survey and other international studies have demonstrated that prioritizing large-scale SARS-CoV-2 vaccination contributed to a reduction of COVID-19-related mortality, decreasing it from approximately 30% in the pre-vaccination era to around 10%–15% after vaccination was introduced (54–57). This shift may be partly related to the more favorable and less aggressive biological behavior of the virus itself, but it is certainly also partly due to patient vaccination and increasing numbers of vaccine doses (57, 58). However, as the presented data shows, a substantial proportion of patients with hematological neoplasms develop measurable vaccine-induced antibody responses following vaccination and, when indicated, booster doses. The likelihood and magnitude of such responses vary substantially according to the underlying malignancy, previous and ongoing anticancer therapy, timing of vaccination and other patient-related and disease-related factors. Nevertheless, the available clinical evidence supports vaccination as an important component of infection prevention in this high-risk population. 8.Optimal vaccination timing in patients with hematological neoplasmsWhenever feasible, patients should receive up-to-date seasonal vaccines and other recommended vaccinations 2–4 weeks before treatment initiation, to allow for an adequate immune response. Prior to vaccination, it is necessary to check the patient's previous vaccination status, and data regarding previous VZV infection/VZV serology and HBV serum markers. Notably, if vaccination cannot be administered within this optimal timeframe due to the urgency or ongoing nature of cancer therapy, it should still be strongly recommended early during treatment (59). Therefore, it is highly important that as soon as a hematological malignancy is suspected, the hematologist immediately refers the patient to receive vaccination, in parallel with performing diagnostic procedures and staging the disease. Unfortunately, in clinical practice, the important vaccination step is often forgotten amid the desire to quickly complete the diagnostic processes. A systematic review and meta-analysis suggested that morning vaccination may enhance antibody responses in adults aged ≥60 years, although these findings were derived from immunocompetent populations. Whether optimizing vaccination according to circadian rhythms improves vaccine immunogenicity or clinical protection in patients with hematological malignancies remains uncertain (60). 9.Vaccination of medical staff and household contacts of patients with hematological neoplasmsHealthcare workers in direct contact with patients or their materials should be vaccinated according to national guidelines or institutional policies, with different vaccines against a range of pathogens, including MMR, BCG, hepatitis B, VZV, pertussis, influenza, COVID-19, and tetanus/diphtheria/polio. Likewise, household contacts of patients should be vaccinated in accordance with international or national guidelines, as this is an important means of preventing some infectious diseases in hematological patients. For example, the guidelines of the Croatian Cooperative Group for Hematological Diseases (KROHEM) recommends that household contacts receive vaccination against SARS-CoV-2, influenza, measles, rubella, mumps, and chickenpox.Evidence from cohorts of healthcare workers also provides useful supporting evidence for the relationship between booster vaccination, humoral and cellular immunity, and breakthrough infection. In a prospective study of healthcare workers, a third dose of mRNA vaccine significantly increased both antibody concentrations and the proportion of participants with detectable IFN-γ responses; however, cellular responses were not independently associated with protection against subsequent SARS-CoV-2 infection (61). Similarly, a large prospective longitudinal study of healthcare workers who received BNT162b2 after two doses of ChAdOx1 found 100% antibody positivity and 92.8% cellular response positivity one month after booster vaccination, while correlations between antibody responses and IFN-γ were weak or negligible, further illustrating that humoral and cellular immunity represent related but partially independent components of vaccine-induced immunity (62). In a separate prospective study of fully vaccinated healthcare workers, breakthrough infections were associated with lower pre-infection neutralizing antibody titers, although most breakthrough infections were mild or asymptomatic (63). Although these studies were conducted predominantly in immunocompetent healthcare workers and therefore cannot be directly extrapolated to hematological patients, they provide relevant evidence that booster vaccination enhances both components of adaptive immunity and that breakthrough infection cannot be predicted based on cellular immunity alone.Notably, oral polio vaccines and live-attenuated influenza vaccines should not be administered to household contacts or healthcare workers who are in contact with hematological patients suffering from malignant hematological diseases, particularly in cases where patients have recently undergone hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or are suffering graft-versus-host disease (59).In some countries, vaccination of healthcare workers is not legally mandated but rests on each individual's decision, while in other countries, vaccination of healthcare workers against selected vaccine-preventable diseases is mandated by law or required as a condition of employment, reflecting its recognized role in protecting both healthcare personnel and vulnerable patients. For healthcare workers, the decision to vaccinate should be understood as a professional obligation and always be subordinated to the well-being of the patients. However, there remains a need for healthcare workers to be further educated about the purpose and safety of vaccination. Notably, there were unfounded concerns among healthcare workers that the COVID-19 vaccine could have negative effects on fertility, which highlights the urgent need for education and provision of relevant medical facts and truthful information. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractVaccination is one of the most successful developments in the history of medicine, having saved countless human lives. Although vaccination is of the utmost importance for patients with hematological neoplasms, it can also be challenging due to the often reduced or absent serological responses. Despite vaccination, breakthrough infections may occur among patients with hematological malignancies, particularly in those with impaired vaccine-induced immune responses. Although humoral responses are frequently impaired, vaccine-induced cellular immunity is preserved in a substantial proportion of patients with hematological malignancies and may contribute to protection against severe infections. Maximizing the immune response to vaccination requires optimal timing of vaccination relative to the administration of antineoplastic therapy. Patients may also fear vaccine side effects and worry that vaccination might influence their cancer therapy. Finally, some medical professionals, family members, and caregivers are insufficiently aware of the importance of vaccination for patients with hematological diseases, as well as their own vaccination. Despite significant developments in the field of vaccination of immunocompromised patients, addressing these challenges will require further high-quality clinical and translational research; continuous education of patients and healthcare providers; and enhanced cooperation and coordination among primary care practitioners, and epidemiological and hematological departments.Keywords: barriers, hematology, immunity, immunocompromised, vaccination
full_text_sections.methods: 4.Breakthrough infection in vaccinated patients with hematological neoplasmsThe above-described results indicate that active infections occur after vaccination in many patients who are undergoing treatment for malignant hematological disease. However, there is a lack of data regarding breakthrough infections (with diseases other than COVID-19) in patients with hematological malignancies.Pagano et al. investigated 1,548 cases of breakthrough COVID-19 infections in adult patients with hematological malignancies, who had received at least one dose of an anti-SARS-CoV-2 vaccine between January 2021 and March 2022. They concluded that although mortality was significantly reduced compared to in the pre-vaccination era, breakthrough COVID-19 in this population was still associated with considerable mortality (42). Similarly, in a retrospective cohort analysis of almost 6,000 hematological patients, Mittelman et al. showed that vaccinated individuals with hematological neoplasms (particularly those undergoing active treatment) experience worse outcomes from breakthrough COVID-19 infections, compared to vaccinated individuals with an intact immune system (43).Wang et al. reported a 13.4% cumulative risk of breakthrough infection among patients with hematological malignancies, ranging from 11.0% in acute lymphocytic leukemia to 17.2% in multiple myeloma, and 17.4% in chronic myeloid leukemia, compared to a significantly lower 4.5% risk among controls. Moreover, hematological patients who experienced breakthrough infections exhibited a 37.8% overall risk of hospitalization, which was markedly higher than the 2.2% risk observed in those without breakthrough infections. Accordingly, the overall mortality risk was 5.7% in patients with breakthrough infections, compared to 0.8% in those without. Together, these findings indicate that, even among fully vaccinated individuals, the risk of breakthrough infections is significantly higher in patients with hematological tumors compared to those without cancer, and that such infections are associated with substantial clinical consequences, including increased rates of hospitalization and mortality (44).A prospective, multicenter, registry-based cohort study conducted in Spain included 1,394 patients with hematological disorders and reported that 37 (2.6%) developed breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infection at a median of 77 days (range 7–195) after full vaccination. Most patients were asymptomatic (19/37, 51.4%), while 19% developed pneumonia, and the overall mortality rate was 8%. In multivariate logistic regression analysis, the absence of detectable antibodies at 3–6 weeks after complete vaccination emerged as the only factor associated with the occurrence of breakthrough infection (45).Piñana et al. also reported that 266 (17%) of 1,551 hematological patients developed breakthrough COVID-19 infection, occurring at a median of 86 days (range 7–391) after full vaccination. Multivariate analysis showed higher rates of breakthrough infection in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (29%) and in those receiving corticosteroids (24.5%), and lower incidence rates in female patients (15.5%) and in those whose last therapy was more than one year ago (14%). Median antibody titers at multiple time-points were significantly lower in patients with breakthrough infections, compared to those without. The cohort exhibited a low SARS-CoV-2-related mortality rate of 1.9% (46). 5.Response to vaccination in patients with hematological neoplasms, according to antineoplastic drugsIn their review, Fattizzo et al. have comprehensively summarized all recent data regarding the impact of different drugs on responses to COVID-19 vaccinations, and other vaccines in the era of targeted therapies (47). Many of the novel targeted therapies used for hematologic disease treatment can exert on-target or off-target immunomodulatory effects, which may influence responses to COVID-19 vaccines, and other vaccines. Agents that predominantly affect B cells—such as anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies, BTK inhibitors, and anti-CD19 CAR T cells—have the most pronounced negative impacts on seroconversion after vaccination, including with vaccines against COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcus, tetanus, and diphtheria toxoid (47). In contrast, JAK2 inhibitors, BCL-2 inhibitors, and hypomethylating agents may reduce immune function, but they appear to have less marked effects on the humoral response to vaccination (47). On the other hand, vaccine efficacy does not seem to be significantly compromised by tyrosine kinase inhibitors used to treat chronic myeloid leukemia and some anti-myeloma therapies, such as proteasome inhibitors and immunomodulatory agents (47). However, reduced seroconversion rates have been observed in patients treated with anti-CD38 and anti-BCMA monoclonal antibodies. Complement inhibitors used for complement-mediated hematologic disorders, and immunosuppressive therapies used for aplastic anemia, generally do not alter seroconversion rates; however, the overall magnitude of the immune response may be diminished in patients receiving steroids or anti-thymocyte globulin (47). 6.Effectiveness of booster doses in patients with hematological neoplasmsRecent studies of vaccination against COVID-19 have documented how booster doses impact the overall immune response after vaccination in immunocompromised patients with hematological tumors (Table 2). Huang et al. demonstrated that among 68 patients with hematologic neoplasms (including lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma, and acute and chronic myeloid leukemia), 89.7% achieved seroconversion following booster vaccination. Multivariate analysis revealed that effective neutralization was independently predicted by the absence of B-cell-targeted therapy within six months before vaccination, and higher immunoglobulin levels. full_text_sections.conclusion: 12.ConclusionPatients with hematological malignancies remain highly vulnerable to infections and represent a heterogeneous population with substantial variation in vaccine-induced immune responses. Although vaccination remains a cornerstone of infection prevention, vaccine-induced immune responses are often impaired in patients with hematological neoplasms, particularly in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and in those receiving B-cell–depleting or B-cell-targeted therapies, including anti-CD20 antibodies, BTK inhibitors, and CAR-T therapy. However, the magnitude of impairment varies according to the several factors, such as underlying disease, disease activity, treatment exposure, timing of vaccination, and degree of immune dysfunction. Among currently available vaccines, RZV currently has the strongest direct evidence for clinical efficacy in patients with hematological malignancies, while pneumococcal, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccines are supported by substantial immunogenicity data and, in several settings, evidence of clinical benefit. Evidence remains limited regarding other vaccines, newer vaccine platforms, and optimal vaccination strategies for patients receiving novel cellular or targeted therapies.Future high-quality clinical and translational studies should therefore prioritize clinically meaningful outcomes, including infection, hospitalization, severe disease, and mortality, in addition to humoral and cellular immunogenicity, to better define vaccine effectiveness and facilitate the development of individualized and more effective vaccination strategies for this vulnerable population.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionPatients with malignant hematological diseases are immunocompromised (1) for several reasons (Table 1). Firstly, hematological tumors affect immunocompetent cells—such as T and B lymphocytes (including plasma cells), neutrophils, macrophages, and antigen-presenting cells—thereby weakening their physiological defense functions. Secondly, the therapies used to treat hematological neoplasms—including standard chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and newer immunotherapy modalities lead to short- or long-term damage and depletion of different immune system components. Thirdly, patients with hematological tumors are often elderly individuals whose immune systems may already be compromised by age and frequent accompanying comorbidities.Table 1Causes of increased risk of infection in hematological patients.Causes of increased risk of infection in hematological patientsUnderlying Disease Direct suppressive effects on innate and acquired immunity (immunocompetent cells, hypogammaglobulinemia)Applied Therapy Direct suppressive effects on innate and acquired immunity (immunocompetent cells, hypogammaglobulinemia)Damage to natural barriers (skin, mucous membranes)Patient Age Immunity naturally compromised by the aging processComorbidities Accompanying diseases further compromise the immunological functions and resistance to pathogensIn patients with hematological neoplasms, infections are the second most common cause of death, following only death from the malignant disease itself. Infections also frequently lead to treatment delays, which negatively impact treatment outcomes and the possibility of achieving remission, and increase the number and length of hospitalizations and the overall treatment costs (2). For example, invasive pneumococcal disease occurs with a 60-fold higher incidence in patients with hematological cancer compared to the healthy population (3). Some studies show that the risk of death from invasive pneumococcal disease is highest among patients with multiple myeloma or chronic lymphocytic leukemia (4). Furthermore, the influenza risk is six-fold higher in patients with multiple myeloma compared to the general population (5). The influenza-attributable mortality rate can reach 9% among hospitalized hematological patients (6), and up to 33% in immunocompromised patients undergoing chemotherapy, compared with 3% among controls (7).The COVID-19 pandemic has brutally highlighted the severity of secondary immunodeficiency in persons with hematological diseases. Patients with hematological tumors exhibited a mortality rate exceeding 30%, which was higher than that among patients with solid malignancies, and almost double the rate in the general population with COVID-19 (8–10). The largest epidemiologic clinical study, EPICOVIDEHA, reported a 31% mortality rate among over 3,000 patients with active hematological malignancy during the first waves of the pandemic (11).Many innovative drugs, particularly various immunotherapy modalities, are being increasingly used in earlier lines of treatment for hematological diseases; which will likely lead to further decreases of mortality. Some currently incurable hematological diseases may even become curable, at least for some patients. These improvements are likely to have unintended consequences, including deeper and longer-lasting immunosuppression and an increased number of various infections.Vaccination is among the greatest achievements in the history of medicine, having saved countless human lives. For patients with hematological tumors, vaccination (e.g., against SARS-CoV-2, influenza, pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, human papilloma virus, hepatitis A and B, chickenpox, herpes zoster, measles, rubella, mumps, respiratory syncytial virus) must be a mandatory part of supportive care, and performed in a timely manner according to the international and national guidelines or the recommendations of health institutions.This manuscript was prepared as a narrative review of the literature on vaccination in adult patients with hematological malignancies. A literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE for studies published from 1989 through 2025 (most of the included publications date from the last five years). Articles published in English were eligible for inclusion. The literature search focused on studies evaluating vaccine immunogenicity, effectiveness, safety and vaccination strategies in adults with hematological malignancies. Priority was given to prospective studies, randomized clinical trials, meta-analyses, and contemporary clinical guidelines. When available, the most recent evidence was preferentially cited. Animal studies, preclinical studies, pediatric-only studies, conference abstracts without full-text publication, duplicate publications, and articles not directly relevant to the review topic were excluded. Studies were selected based on their relevance to the objectives of the review, methodological quality, and clinical significance, with priority given to recent evidence.Unlike previous reviews addressing vaccination in broader populations of immunocompromised patients with cancer, this review focuses exclusively on patients with hematological neoplasms. Although recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses have assessed vaccine immunogenicity and clinical outcomes in this population, our aim is to provide an integrated, clinically oriented overview of the main challenges related to vaccination and potential strategies to overcome them, rather than to discuss the technical indications and schedules of individual vaccines. The relatively greater emphasis on COVID-19 vaccination in this review reflects the current evidence base, as most recent high-quality studies investigating vaccine efficacy, immunogenicity, and safety in patients with hematological malignancies have focused on SARS-CoV-2 vaccines. However, an effort was made to include other vaccines used in hematological patients. 2.Humoral response rates after vaccination in different hematological neoplasmsThe patients with hematological tumors often show lower vaccine-induced antibody responses compared with the general population, due to damage and reduced numbers or function of immunocompetent cells that contribute to the generation of an immune response after vaccination. Importantly, seroconversion and antibody titers are measures of vaccine immunogenicity and should not be automatically interpreted as evidence of clinical protection unless a validated correlation of protection for the specific vaccine and pathogen has been established.In a study of patients with hematological malignancies, Monkman et al. reported a 21% seroconversion rate after H1N1 influenza vaccination, which was significantly higher than that in unvaccinated patients (0%), but significantly lower than that previously reported in healthy adults (12). In their systematic review of the effects of influenza vaccination in patients with hematological diseases, Le Torre et al. analyzed pooled data from 22 studies, including 19 cohort studies, 2 randomized clinical trials, and 1 cross-sectional study from 1993 to 2016. For H1N1, they reported a 30% protection rate after a booster dose. For H3N2 and influenza B, the pooled protection rates after the first vaccination dose were 42.6% and 39.6%, respectively. full_text: While certain forms of lymphoma—such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma—are classified as curable, with over half of all patients achieving remission following first-line therapy, a significant proportion of patients still suffer from relapsed or refractory disease. Through autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy can significantly improve survival rates, their widespread clinical utility is constrained by logistical bottlenecks, manufacturing complexities, and high financial burdens. Similarly, antibody-drug conjugates and bispecific antibodies have achieved striking success against hematologic malignancies, but their clinical adoption is often hindered by the requirement for continuous infusion. Consequently, systemically delivered oncolytic viruses engineered to express immunotherapeutic elements have emerged as highly innovative alternatives. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape and outlines the therapeutic potential of oncolytic virotherapy in the fight against hematopoietic malignancies. We cross-examined a robust dataset of over 100 preclinical investigations to critically assess the therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles of more than ten diverse oncolytic virus platforms developed for blood cancer treatment, alongside multiple early-phase clinical trials that are completed or currently underway. By synthesizing these preclinical and clinical data, we propose three critical development pathways—enhancing target specificity, arming viral vectors, and designing synergistic combination regimens—to accelerate the translation of clinically viable oncolytic viruses for hematologic oncology. Introduction and methodologyOncolytic viruses (OVs) have been widely studied in solid tumors, typically through intratumoral administration. In contrast, hematopoietic malignancies—which inherently require systemic drug delivery rather than local injection—have historically received less attention as primary targets for OV therapy. In this review, we explored data from clinical applications and trials, tracing evidence back through preclinical and basic research. By analyzing the current landscape of utilizing OVs to treat hematopoietic malignancies, we highlight this systemic targeting paradigm as possessing a uniquely favorable therapeutic window for advanced OV research.This mini-review was conducted by searching the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases up to July 2026 using the terms “oncolytic virus” and “hematopoietic malignancies” or “blood cancer” or “lymphoma” or “leukemia” or “multiple myeloma.” Additional references were identified through citation tracking of relevant reviews and primary studies, prioritizing the most recent and clinically significant trials, preclinical advances, and mechanistic insights.Inclusion criteria: Studies were included if they evaluated live oncolytic virus platforms specifically targeting hematopoietic malignancies, lymphomas, leukemias, or multiple myeloma in preclinical models or clinical trials. Only articles published in English were considered, with no restrictions applied to publication date or study type.Exclusion criteria: Non-English articles, abstract-only publications lacking primary data, and studies focusing strictly on solid tumors without hematological evaluations were excluded.Initial database searches yielded a combined pool of records. Duplicates were removed, and the remaining articles were screened by the first reviewer based on title and abstract. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were then independently assessed against the inclusion criteria by a second reviewer. Any discrepancies regarding article selection or data extraction were resolved through consensus discussion between both reviewers prior to final inclusion Supplementary Tables and Figure 1. For each eligible study, information regarding study design, disease indication, efficacy-related outcomes, safety profiles, and adverse events associated with oncolytic virotherapy was collected and summarized.Figure 1Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers. Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers recorded in the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases in the past three decades are distributed according to the publication year (X-axis) and virus types (Y-axis). For preclinical studies, the numbers inside the blue circles indicate the number of studies conducted for each OV in that year; those without numbers indicate that only one study was conducted. The Pteropine orthoreovirus (Sikamat virus) grouped under ‘Other’ is a distinct bat-borne species and not the mammalian reovirus (pelareorep) shown as ‘Reovirus’. Detail information was collected in Supplementary Tables 1, 2, from which the figure was generated using Python (Matplotlib).Scatter plot showing years of publication for studies on various oncolytic viruses from 1995 to 2025. Blue circles represent pre-clinical studies, and red stars denote clinical studies or case reports. Each row corresponds to a different virus, including measles virus, adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus, reovirus, vaccinia virus, myxoma virus, Newcastle disease virus, herpes simplex virus, and others. Most clinical studies occur after 2015, with recent entries for SARS-CoV-2. A legend specifies the meaning of symbols. The start: clinical case reports of tumor regressions after virus infectionThe therapeutic potential of viruses in oncology was initially inferred from clinical observations of spontaneous tumor regression following naturally acquired viral infections. Notably, transient remissions in patients with leukemia and lymphoma were historically reported during concurrent influenza or measles virus (MV) infections. More recently, similar remissions have been documented in hematologic malignancies following severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. The inherent tumor-selectivity demonstrated by many wild-type viruses is largely attributed to the altered cellular landscape of neoplastic cells. Specifically, the hallmarks of cancer create a permissive microenvironment that overlaps significantly with cellular features required for efficient viral replication. Oncolytic viruses: a new generation of live cancer cell killersOVs are replication-competent, biologically active agents that exert anti-cancer effects through two principal mechanisms: direct tumor cell lysis and indirect stimulation of systemic anti-tumor immunity. In hematologic malignancies, where cancer cells reside in immune-privileged niches such as the bone marrow or peripheral blood, this dual functionality is particularly advantageous. On one hand, OVs themselves exploit molecular vulnerabilities in malignant cells; on the other hand, OVs can be armed with immunomodulatory transgenes to amplify their therapeutic impact. Pre-clinical studies on evaluating therapeutic OVs in blood cancersTo comprehensively examine and summarize the existing literature regarding OVs in blood cancer therapy and explore treatment-related outcomes, we first retrieved citations using the terms indicated in the Methodology section. After the title and abstract screening phase, the non-overlapping research articles were combined and analyzed. Then we grouped these studies according to the different virus types. Among them, MV was the most frequently studied in publications, followed by adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and reovirus (Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Below, we will analyze the study setup and major outcomes of these studies based on different OV types.Although adenovirus was the most frequently applied one in clinical trials,1 only a handful of studies were performed in blood cancer treatment. These studies ranged from systematic evaluation to rational design of human adenoviruses for enhanced blood cancer therapy. In an earlier study by Qian and colleagues, E1B55K-deleted adenovirus type 5 (Ad5) armed with melanoma differentiation-associated gene-7/interleukin-24 (MDA-7/IL-24) was tested in a range of blood cancer cell lines. Although a potent anti-cancer effect was observed in vitro and in vivo, the effect was limited to Ad5 major receptor (coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor)-expressing hematological malignancies (Qian et al., 2008). Follow-up studies solved the problem by using chimeric Ad35 fiber (Wang et al., 2009; Wenthe et al., 2020). Another study compared the growth-inhibition effect of adenovirus and herpes simplex virus (HSV) on several cell lines; HSV was more effective (Zhang et al., 2011). Realizing the limitation from Ad5, a broad range of human adenoviruses were evaluated by Barry’s research group. They observed robust killing and delayed lymphoma growth by species D adenoviruses (Chen et al., 2011). However, in mouse B cell lymphoma model A20, only prophylactic immunization by adenovirus against A20 tumors can protect against A20 lymphomas; established A20 tumors were not controlled by A20-expressing adenovirus immunization (Weaver et al., 2011). While OV alone is not enough to control blood malignancies, a combination approach highlights the optimized development strategy. A rationally designed OAd5F35, Ad5-based chimeric virus with Ad35 fiber, armed with TMZ-CD40L and 4-1BBL was evaluated in combination with CAR-T therapy. The fiber switch to Ad35 enabled the use of CD46, which is up-regulated in hematological malignancies, thereby enhancing targeting and replication. Interestingly, OAd5F35 infection induced transgene expression and a change in immune markers. In combination with CAR-T therapy, the infected lymphoma cells were found to secrete chemokines to attract CAR-T cells, thereby increased CAR-T cell activation was observed. Importantly, the enhanced lymphoma cell killing was also observed in vivo in xenograft models (Wenthe et al., 2021). Similarly, a CD47 antibody expressing adenovirus (Ad5-hTert-E1A-IRES-E1B with mCMV-mCD47nb-Fc) as in situ tumor vaccination also showed positive immune-regulation and protection from tumor re-challenge (Zhang et al., 2022). These data suggested that adenovirus alone is not enough to control such aggressive hematological malignancies; a combination approach should be the development strategy of choice.Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC), based on HSV-1, is so far the only OV approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of melanoma (Zhang T. et al., 2023). However, only a few studies have explored its potential in hematological malignancies. In the search for molecular indicators for permissiveness to HSV therapy, transcription factors downstream of Ras were evaluated in non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) cell lines infected with R3616, an HSV-1 with a deletion of the viral γ134.5 gene. Ras signaling was assessed by immunoblotting for different downstream effectors, which revealed ERK/ELK as a suitable predictive indicator for selection of cancer cells with increased sensitivity to HSV-based therapy (Esfandyari et al., 2009). As G47Δ was approved in Japan in 2021 (Frampton, 2022), a similar version of this OV was evaluated in a broad panel of 26 cell lines and 15 primary cells derived from various lineages of hematological malignancies (Ishino et al., 2021). The expression of an HSV-1 receptor, nectin-1, was identified as a determining factor in the oncolytic effect determined by viral entry and cytotoxicity. Although only a low level of virus replication was detected in hematological cancer cells, the virus could induce immunogenic cell death and kill the malignant cells. Importantly, this study demonstrated that systemic tumor-specific CD8 + T cell responses efficiently concentrated at tumor sites, suggesting that local intratumoral injection of HSV-1 is expected to provoke effective immune responses even for systemic tumors such as hematological malignancies. Recently, an oncolytic type II HSV (oHSV2) was explored in the treatment of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (Zhang J. et al., 2023). In comparison with the clinical chemotherapeutic drug doxorubicin (DOX), oHSV2 revealed a better therapeutic profile on the apoptotic, invasive, and proliferative capacity of DLBCL cells in vitro. Moreover, oHSV2 can also inhibit transplanted tumor growth and accelerate CD4 + T and CD8 + T cell infiltration in mice, with an acceptable safety profile in the organs of tumor-bearing animals. To explore the potential of combination therapy with immune-checkpoint inhibitors, this study also showed oHSV2 can inhibit the PD-1/PD-L1 immune-checkpoint, thereby restraining cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) apoptosis and encouraging CTL proliferation. The combination therapy resulted in enhanced killing of malignant cells and inhibited tumor growth in mice. Similar to the adenovirus studies, combination therapy and the individual receptor profile are essential for further HSV application in hematological malignancies.The rat protoparvovirus H-1 (H-1PV) does not infect or cause any disease in humans, but has natural tropism for human cancer cells. H-1PV demonstrates a broad range of anticancer activities in several preclinical cancer models and in clinical trials (Geletneky et al., 2017; Bretscher and Marchini, 2019; Hajda et al., 2021). The first study to apply H-1PV to Burkitt’s lymphoma (BL)-derived cell lines showed high sensitivity to H-1PV-induced oncolysis in vitro. The H-1PV infection of BL lines is productive and leads to predominantly necrotic cell death. Importantly, normal B cells from healthy donors are resistant to H-1PV infection (Angelova et al., 2009). Then a large panel of lymphoma- and leukemia-derived cell lines was included to assess the capacity of H-1PV to target hematological malignancies. This study revealed that most cell lines are sensitive to H-1PV-induced cell death, and the progeny virion production, rather than virus entry, was the determining factor. Among all tested cells, DLBCL cells supported high levels of H-1PV progeny virion production and were almost totally eradicated by very low virus doses. Moreover, DLBCL cell lines with upregulated expression of aldehyde dehydrogenase 1A1 conferring chemotherapy resistance were among the most sensitive H-1PV targets (Angelova et al., 2017). A recent study extended this work to cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). H-1PV infects and induces oncolysis in both classically grown CTCL suspension cultures and in a novel, in vivo-relevant, heterotypic spheroid model, but not in healthy donor controls, including peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). In CTCL spheroid co-cultures with PBMCs, treatment with the virus increased infiltration of the spheroids with immune cells (Angelova et al., 2024).Among oncolytic platforms, MV is the most extensively studied in hematological malignancies, owing to its vaccine safety record and its natural tropism for CD46 and the lymphocyte receptor SLAM/CD150 (Ong et al., 2006; Engeland and Ungerechts, 2021). Vaccine-strain MV was found to regress human B-cell lymphoma xenografts even in the presence of anti-MV antibodies (Grote et al., 2001). Subsequent improvement in specificity was achieved by retargeting viral entry. Vectors retargeted to CD20, armed with a prodrug convertase, and combined with cyclophosphamide and fludarabine regressed mantle cell lymphoma xenografts, though with limited survival benefit (Bucheit et al., 2003; Ungerechts et al., 2010). Analogous CD30 and CD38 retargeting extended the approach to Hodgkin lymphoma and myeloma (Peng et al., 2003; Hanauer et al., 2018). Importantly, efficacy was tracked with receptor usage and innate signaling. For instance, SLAM-dependent entry in mantle cell lymphoma virotherapy, EBV-driven CD150 upregulation and type I interferon responsiveness have been shown to determine susceptibility, and Bcl-2 has been shown to slow oncolysis in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (Patel et al., 2011; Miest et al., 2013; Fernandez et al., 2014; Takeda et al., 2014). To facilitate systemic delivery in the face of anti-MV immunity, studies have shown that both carrier and mesenchymal stromal cells have the capacity to deliver the virus to sites of disseminated disease (Iankov et al., 2007; Castleton et al., 2014). In particular, the development of the thyroidal sodium iodide symporter-expressing MV-NIS has advanced MV into early-phase clinical testing for multiple myeloma (MM) (Dingli et al., 2004).Vaccinia virus (VV), a large-genome poxvirus that tolerates sizeable transgene insertions, has been used in blood cancers mainly as an arming and combination platform rather than as a bare oncolytic agent. An attenuated VV delivered by cytokine-induced killer cells trafficked to residual murine B-cell lymphoma and prevented relapse through acquired antitumor immunity (Contag et al., 2010). Its coding capacity has since carried both pro-apoptotic and immunomodulatory transgenes. Notably, immune-arming constructs have been developed to combine oncolysis with a defined effector mechanism. A CD19 bispecific T-cell engager recruited T cells, an anti-CD47 nanobody reprogrammed macrophages, and interleukin-18 relieved T-cell exhaustion, each prolonging survival in lymphoma models (Lei et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026).
