full_text_sections.abstract: While certain forms of lymphoma—such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma—are classified as curable, with over half of all patients achieving remission following first-line therapy, a significant proportion of patients still suffer from relapsed or refractory disease. Through autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy can significantly improve survival rates, their widespread clinical utility is constrained by logistical bottlenecks, manufacturing complexities, and high financial burdens. Similarly, antibody-drug conjugates and bispecific antibodies have achieved striking success against hematologic malignancies, but their clinical adoption is often hindered by the requirement for continuous infusion. Consequently, systemically delivered oncolytic viruses engineered to express immunotherapeutic elements have emerged as highly innovative alternatives. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape and outlines the therapeutic potential of oncolytic virotherapy in the fight against hematopoietic malignancies. We cross-examined a robust dataset of over 100 preclinical investigations to critically assess the therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles of more than ten diverse oncolytic virus platforms developed for blood cancer treatment, alongside multiple early-phase clinical trials that are completed or currently underway. By synthesizing these preclinical and clinical data, we propose three critical development pathways—enhancing target specificity, arming viral vectors, and designing synergistic combination regimens—to accelerate the translation of clinically viable oncolytic viruses for hematologic oncology.
full_text_sections.methods: Introduction and methodologyOncolytic viruses (OVs) have been widely studied in solid tumors, typically through intratumoral administration. In contrast, hematopoietic malignancies—which inherently require systemic drug delivery rather than local injection—have historically received less attention as primary targets for OV therapy. In this review, we explored data from clinical applications and trials, tracing evidence back through preclinical and basic research. By analyzing the current landscape of utilizing OVs to treat hematopoietic malignancies, we highlight this systemic targeting paradigm as possessing a uniquely favorable therapeutic window for advanced OV research.This mini-review was conducted by searching the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases up to July 2026 using the terms “oncolytic virus” and “hematopoietic malignancies” or “blood cancer” or “lymphoma” or “leukemia” or “multiple myeloma.” Additional references were identified through citation tracking of relevant reviews and primary studies, prioritizing the most recent and clinically significant trials, preclinical advances, and mechanistic insights.Inclusion criteria: Studies were included if they evaluated live oncolytic virus platforms specifically targeting hematopoietic malignancies, lymphomas, leukemias, or multiple myeloma in preclinical models or clinical trials. Only articles published in English were considered, with no restrictions applied to publication date or study type.Exclusion criteria: Non-English articles, abstract-only publications lacking primary data, and studies focusing strictly on solid tumors without hematological evaluations were excluded.Initial database searches yielded a combined pool of records. Duplicates were removed, and the remaining articles were screened by the first reviewer based on title and abstract. Full texts of potentially eligible studies were then independently assessed against the inclusion criteria by a second reviewer. Any discrepancies regarding article selection or data extraction were resolved through consensus discussion between both reviewers prior to final inclusion Supplementary Tables and Figure 1. For each eligible study, information regarding study design, disease indication, efficacy-related outcomes, safety profiles, and adverse events associated with oncolytic virotherapy was collected and summarized.Figure 1Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers. Pre-clinical and clinical studies using OVs to treat blood cancers recorded in the PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases in the past three decades are distributed according to the publication year (X-axis) and virus types (Y-axis). For preclinical studies, the numbers inside the blue circles indicate the number of studies conducted for each OV in that year; those without numbers indicate that only one study was conducted. The Pteropine orthoreovirus (Sikamat virus) grouped under ‘Other’ is a distinct bat-borne species and not the mammalian reovirus (pelareorep) shown as ‘Reovirus’. Detail information was collected in Supplementary Tables 1, 2, from which the figure was generated using Python (Matplotlib).Scatter plot showing years of publication for studies on various oncolytic viruses from 1995 to 2025. Blue circles represent pre-clinical studies, and red stars denote clinical studies or case reports. Each row corresponds to a different virus, including measles virus, adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus, reovirus, vaccinia virus, myxoma virus, Newcastle disease virus, herpes simplex virus, and others. Most clinical studies occur after 2015, with recent entries for SARS-CoV-2. A legend specifies the meaning of symbols.
full_text_sections.other: The start: clinical case reports of tumor regressions after virus infectionThe therapeutic potential of viruses in oncology was initially inferred from clinical observations of spontaneous tumor regression following naturally acquired viral infections. Notably, transient remissions in patients with leukemia and lymphoma were historically reported during concurrent influenza or measles virus (MV) infections. More recently, similar remissions have been documented in hematologic malignancies following severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. The inherent tumor-selectivity demonstrated by many wild-type viruses is largely attributed to the altered cellular landscape of neoplastic cells. Specifically, the hallmarks of cancer create a permissive microenvironment that overlaps significantly with cellular features required for efficient viral replication. Oncolytic viruses: a new generation of live cancer cell killersOVs are replication-competent, biologically active agents that exert anti-cancer effects through two principal mechanisms: direct tumor cell lysis and indirect stimulation of systemic anti-tumor immunity. In hematologic malignancies, where cancer cells reside in immune-privileged niches such as the bone marrow or peripheral blood, this dual functionality is particularly advantageous. On one hand, OVs themselves exploit molecular vulnerabilities in malignant cells; on the other hand, OVs can be armed with immunomodulatory transgenes to amplify their therapeutic impact. Pre-clinical studies on evaluating therapeutic OVs in blood cancersTo comprehensively examine and summarize the existing literature regarding OVs in blood cancer therapy and explore treatment-related outcomes, we first retrieved citations using the terms indicated in the Methodology section. After the title and abstract screening phase, the non-overlapping research articles were combined and analyzed. Then we grouped these studies according to the different virus types. Among them, MV was the most frequently studied in publications, followed by adenovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and reovirus (Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Below, we will analyze the study setup and major outcomes of these studies based on different OV types.Although adenovirus was the most frequently applied one in clinical trials,1 only a handful of studies were performed in blood cancer treatment. These studies ranged from systematic evaluation to rational design of human adenoviruses for enhanced blood cancer therapy. In an earlier study by Qian and colleagues, E1B55K-deleted adenovirus type 5 (Ad5) armed with melanoma differentiation-associated gene-7/interleukin-24 (MDA-7/IL-24) was tested in a range of blood cancer cell lines. Although a potent anti-cancer effect was observed in vitro and in vivo, the effect was limited to Ad5 major receptor (coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor)-expressing hematological malignancies (Qian et al., 2008). Follow-up studies solved the problem by using chimeric Ad35 fiber (Wang et al., 2009; Wenthe et al., 2020). Another study compared the growth-inhibition effect of adenovirus and herpes simplex virus (HSV) on several cell lines; HSV was more effective (Zhang et al., 2011). Realizing the limitation from Ad5, a broad range of human adenoviruses were evaluated by Barry’s research group. They observed robust killing and delayed lymphoma growth by species D adenoviruses (Chen et al., 2011). However, in mouse B cell lymphoma model A20, only prophylactic immunization by adenovirus against A20 tumors can protect against A20 lymphomas; established A20 tumors were not controlled by A20-expressing adenovirus immunization (Weaver et al., 2011). While OV alone is not enough to control blood malignancies, a combination approach highlights the optimized development strategy. A rationally designed OAd5F35, Ad5-based chimeric virus with Ad35 fiber, armed with TMZ-CD40L and 4-1BBL was evaluated in combination with CAR-T therapy. The fiber switch to Ad35 enabled the use of CD46, which is up-regulated in hematological malignancies, thereby enhancing targeting and replication. Interestingly, OAd5F35 infection induced transgene expression and a change in immune markers. In combination with CAR-T therapy, the infected lymphoma cells were found to secrete chemokines to attract CAR-T cells, thereby increased CAR-T cell activation was observed. However, only a few studies have explored its potential in hematological malignancies. title_original: Therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in hematopoietic malignancies: from preclinical insights to clinical realities

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses (OVs) in hematopoietic malignancies, addressing the limitations of current treatments like autologous stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy. The research sought to evaluate the efficacy and safety profiles of OVs targeting hematological cancers, including lymphomas, leukemias, and multiple myeloma, through preclinical and early-phase clinical trials.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A systematic review was conducted by searching PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov databases up to July 2026, using terms related to oncolytic viruses and hematopoietic malignancies. The study included preclinical models and clinical trials evaluating live OVs targeting hematological cancers, with a focus on recent and clinically significant trials and mechanistic insights.
analysis.methods: The review included a comprehensive analysis of over 100 preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials, evaluating various OVs such as adenovirus, measles virus, and herpes simplex virus (HSV). Methods involved assessing therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles, including immunogenic cell death, immune regulation, and combination therapies with checkpoint inhibitors.
analysis.main_results: The review found that OVs showed therapeutic potential in hematopoietic malignancies, with some studies demonstrating improved outcomes when combined with other therapies. For instance, HSV-1 showed better therapeutic profiles compared to doxorubicin in vitro, and measles virus was found to be highly sensitive to oncolysis in Burkitt’s lymphoma cell lines.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating the potential of OVs in hematopoietic malignancies, particularly when combined with other therapies. Novel insights included the ability of OVs to induce immunogenic cell death and to enhance immune responses, suggesting a favorable therapeutic window for advanced OV research.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of new treatment strategies for hematopoietic malignancies, potentially improving patient outcomes and reducing the reliance on costly and logistically challenging therapies like CAR T-cell therapy.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the reliance on preclinical data and early-phase clinical trials, which may not fully represent the complexities of human disease. The evidence strength is moderate due to the variability in study designs and the need for further clinical validation.

analysis.summary_en: This review assessed the therapeutic potential of oncolytic viruses in hematopoietic malignancies, highlighting their efficacy and safety profiles in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. The findings suggest potential improvements in treatment strategies for hematological cancers, particularly when combined with other therapies.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估溶瘤病毒(OVs)在血液恶性肿瘤中的治疗潜力,解决当前如自体干细胞移植和嵌合抗原受体(CAR)T细胞疗法等治疗手段的局限性。研究旨在通过预临床和早期临床试验评估OVs针对血液系统癌症(包括淋巴瘤、白血病和多发性骨髓瘤)的疗效和安全性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本系统综述通过在PubMed和ClinicalTrials.gov数据库中使用与溶瘤病毒和血液恶性肿瘤相关的术语进行检索,截至2026年7月。研究包括了评估活OVs治疗血液系统癌症的预临床模型和临床试验,重点是最近和临床意义重大的试验和机制见解。
elements_zh.methods: 综述包括了对超过100项预临床研究和早期临床试验的全面分析,评估了腺病毒、麻疹病毒和单纯疱疹病毒(HSV)等多种OVs。方法包括评估治疗疗效和安全性,包括免疫细胞死亡、免疫调节和与检查点抑制剂的联合疗法。
elements_zh.main_results: 综述发现,OVs在血液恶性肿瘤中显示出治疗潜力,一些研究显示与其他疗法联合使用时可以改善结果。例如,HSV-1在体外显示了更好的治疗效果,而麻疹病毒在Burkitt淋巴瘤细胞系中对溶瘤作用高度敏感。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释了这些发现表明OVs在血液恶性肿瘤中的潜力,特别是在与其他疗法联合使用时。新颖的见解包括OVs能够诱导免疫细胞死亡并增强免疫应答,这表明高级OV研究具有有利的治疗窗口。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为血液恶性肿瘤的新治疗策略提供信息,可能改善患者结果并减少对昂贵且物流复杂的CAR T细胞疗法的依赖。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 研究的局限性包括依赖于预临床数据和早期临床试验,这可能无法完全代表人类疾病的复杂性。证据强度中等,因为研究设计的差异性和需要进一步的临床验证。

summary_zh: 本综述提供了当前溶瘤病毒治疗在对抗血液恶性肿瘤方面的全面概述。在本综述中,我们探讨了临床应用和试验中的数据,追溯证据至预临床和基础研究。通过分析利用溶瘤病毒(OVs)治疗血液恶性肿瘤的现状,我们强调了这种全身靶向模式具有独特的有利治疗窗口,适合高级OV研究。本迷你综述通过在PubMed和ClinicalTrials.gov数据库中使用“溶瘤病毒”和“血液恶性肿瘤”或“血液癌症”或“淋巴瘤”或“白血病”或“多发性骨髓瘤”等术语进行检索,截至2026年7月。通过引用相关综述和原始研究的引用追踪,我们确定了额外的参考文献,优先考虑最近和临床意义重大的试验、预临床进展和机制见解。纳入标准:研究如果评估了专门针对血液恶性肿瘤、淋巴瘤、白血病或多发性骨髓瘤的活溶瘤病毒平台,则被纳入。尽管某些类型的淋巴瘤——如经典霍奇金淋巴瘤——被归类为可治愈的,超过一半的患者在接受一线治疗后达到缓解,但仍有相当一部分患者仍遭受复发或难治性疾病。通过自体干细胞移植(ASCT)和嵌合抗原受体(CAR)T细胞疗法可以显著提高生存率,但其临床应用受到物流瓶颈、制造复杂性和高昂的财务负担的限制。同样,抗体药物偶联物和双特异性抗体等治疗方法也存在类似的挑战。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估溶瘤病毒(OVs)在血液恶性肿瘤中的治疗潜力,解决当前如自体干细胞移植和嵌合抗原受体(CAR)T细胞疗法等治疗手段的局限性。研究旨在通过预临床和早期临床试验评估OVs针对血液系统癌症(包括淋巴瘤、白血病和多发性骨髓瘤)的疗效和安全性。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本系统综述通过在PubMed和ClinicalTrials.gov数据库中使用与溶瘤病毒和血液恶性肿瘤相关的术语进行检索,截至2026年7月。研究包括了评估活OVs治疗血液系统癌症的预临床模型和临床试验,重点是最近和临床意义重大的试验和机制见解。
analysis_zh.methods: 综述包括了对超过100项预临床研究和早期临床试验的全面分析,评估了腺病毒、麻疹病毒和单纯疱疹病毒(HSV)等多种OVs。方法包括评估治疗疗效和安全性,包括免疫细胞死亡、免疫调节和与检查点抑制剂的联合疗法。
analysis_zh.main_results: 综述发现,OVs在血液恶性肿瘤中显示出治疗潜力,一些研究显示与其他疗法联合使用时可以改善结果。例如,HSV-1在体外显示了更好的治疗效果,而麻疹病毒在Burkitt淋巴瘤细胞系中对溶瘤作用高度敏感。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释了这些发现表明OVs在血液恶性肿瘤中的潜力,特别是在与其他疗法联合使用时。新颖的见解包括OVs能够诱导免疫细胞死亡并增强免疫应答,这表明高级OV研究具有有利的治疗窗口。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为血液恶性肿瘤的新治疗策略提供信息,可能改善患者结果并减少对昂贵且物流复杂的CAR T细胞疗法的依赖。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 研究的局限性包括依赖于预临床数据和早期临床试验,这可能无法完全代表人类疾病的复杂性。证据强度中等,因为研究设计的差异性和需要进一步的临床验证。

title: Application and prospects of veterinary diagnostic techniques in laboratory monkeys

source_records.title: Application and prospects of veterinary diagnostic techniques in laboratory monkeys
Application and prospects of veterinary diagnostic techniques in laboratory monkeys

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: As the non-human primate models with the closest genetic relationship to humans, laboratory monkeys are indispensable in life sciences research, drug development, and biological product evaluation. However, infectious diseases either endemic in laboratory monkey colonies or acquired during breeding and husbandry—for example, B virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis-threaten animal welfare and colony security, while also elevating zoonotic transmission risks and compromising the reliability of research data. The diversity, complexity, and clinically insidious nature of diseases in laboratory monkeys impose stringent demands on veterinary diagnostic capabilities. This review summarizes the current status and recent advances in mainstream veterinary diagnostic techniques applied to laboratory monkey disease surveillance. Building on these advances, we further identify practical bottlenecks in diagnostic deployment and propose targeted countermeasures. Finally, we explore emerging trends and application prospects for point-of-care testing, multiplex pathogen detection, and artificial intelligence-assisted diagnosis, which collectively support the development of accurate, efficient, and intelligent disease diagnostics for laboratory monkeys. These infections may manifest as overt diseases or remain in latent or subclinical states (9–12). Gastrointestinal parasites have also been documented in macaque populations, with potential zoonotic implications (13).The presence of infectious diseases in laboratory monkeys directly compromises their animal welfare and health, affecting the stability and breeding of the population. Latent infections with pathogens may serve as uncontrolled confounding variables in experimental studies, impairing the accuracy, reproducibility, and reliability of research outcomes. For example, co-infection rates of SIV with measles virus or Toxoplasma gondii have been documented at 10~30% in certain colonies (9–12, 17). However, infectious diseases either endemic in laboratory monkey colonies or acquired during breeding and husbandry—for example, B virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis-threaten animal welfare and colony security, while also elevating zoonotic transmission risks and compromising the reliability of research data. By comparing these techniques across sensitivity, specificity, cost-effectiveness, and operational feasibility, we delineate their suitability for distinct use cases: high-precision laboratory testing, large-scale colony screening, and point-of-care clinical diagnosis. Current veterinary diagnostic assays for laboratory monkeys achieve robust analytical performance. In several studies, qPCR delivers 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for B virus detection, digital PCR (dPCR) attains a limit of detection as low as 45 copies/ml for monkeypox virus; and CRISPR/Cas-based assays have demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in clinical validation cohorts. Building on these advances, we further identify practical bottlenecks in diagnostic deployment and propose targeted countermeasures. Finally, we explore emerging trends and application prospects for point-of-care testing, multiplex pathogen detection, and artificial intelligence-assisted diagnosis, which collectively support the development of accurate, efficient, and intelligent disease diagnostics for laboratory monkeys. This work aims to provide a theoretical and practical reference for clinical practice and scientific research focused on laboratory monkey disease prevention and control.

elements_en.research_question_and_background: Immunochromatographic techniques, such as colloidal gold test strips and immunoassay combs, play an important role in on-site rapid screening owing to their simplicity and lack of equipment requirements (27).
elements_en.study_design_and_population: First, prospective validation studies with standardized protocols and well-defined reference standards are urgently needed to establish the true performance of new diagnostic platforms under real-world conditions.
elements_en.methods: In several studies, qPCR delivers 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for B virus detection, digital PCR (dPCR) attains a limit of detection as low as 45 copies/ml for monkeypox virus; and CRISPR/Cas-based assays have demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in clinical validation cohorts.
elements_en.main_results: Concurrent infections with B virus and SIV have also been reported, with B virus seroprevalence reaching 80~90% in adult macaques.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: They are gradually being replaced by novel immunological methods such as ELISA (23).
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: They contribute to zoonotic disease prevention by identifying infected animals before transmission occurs, and to biosafety and biosecurity by containing pathogens at their source.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Furthermore, accurate diagnostics enhance public-health surveillance for emerging zoonotic threats and ensure the reliability of biomedical research by maintaining specific-pathogen-free colonies and preventing undetected infections from confounding experimental data.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 首先,迫切需要进行前瞻性验证研究,采用标准化协议和明确的参考标准,以在真实世界条件下建立新诊断平台的真实性能。
elements_zh.methods: 在多项研究中,qPCR对B病毒检测表现出100%的敏感性和100%的特异性,数字PCR(dPCR)对猴痘病毒的检测限低至45 copies/ml;基于CRISPR/Cas的检测方法在临床验证队列研究中也表现出100%的敏感性和100%的特异性。
elements_zh.main_results: B病毒与SIV的并发感染也已被报道,其中B病毒血清流行率在成年猕猴中达到80~90%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 它们正逐渐被新型免疫学方法如ELISA(23)所取代。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 它们通过在传播发生前识别感染动物,有助于人兽共患病的预防,并通过在源头控制病原体,有助于生物安全和生物安保。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 此外,准确的诊断有助于应对新兴人兽共患病威胁的公共卫生监测,并通过维持无特定病原体的群体和防止未检测到的感染干扰实验数据,确保生物医学研究的可靠性。

title_zh: 兽医诊断技术在实验猴中的应用与前景
source_body_en: This review summarizes the current status and recent advances in mainstream veterinary diagnostic techniques applied to laboratory monkey disease surveillance. We analyze the specific applications, strengths, and limitations of molecular, immunological, imaging, and conventional microbiological methods for detecting major viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens of laboratory monkeys, covering quantitative PCR (qPCR), CRISPR-based assays, ELISA, IFA/IHC, and other established platforms. Several key takeaways emerge from this review with direct practical implications.First, no single diagnostic technique is universally applicable. The choice of diagnostic method should be guided by the specific pathogen (e.g., bacterial, viral, or parasitic), sample type (e.g., blood, BALF, or tissue), and clinical scenario (e.g., routine screening, outbreak investigation, or confirmatory diagnosis). Third, cost-effectiveness analyses should be conducted to inform practical deployment decisions, particularly for resource-limited settings where advanced technologies may be prohibitively expensive.In conclusion, the future of laboratory monkey diagnostics lies not in replacing established methods with emerging technologies, but in their strategic integration. As the non-human primate models with the closest genetic relationship to humans, laboratory monkeys are indispensable in life sciences research, drug development, and biological product evaluation. However, infectious diseases either endemic in laboratory monkey colonies or acquired during breeding and husbandry—for example, B virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis-threaten animal welfare and colony security, while also elevating zoonotic transmission risks and compromising the reliability of research data. abstract_zh: 本综述总结了主流兽医诊断技术在实验室猴疾病监测中的当前状况和最新进展。我们分析了分子、免疫学、成像和传统微生物学方法在检测实验室猴主要病毒、细菌和寄生虫病原体中的具体应用、优势和局限性,涵盖了定量PCR(qPCR)、基于CRISPR的检测方法、ELISA、IFA/IHC以及其他已建立的平台。从本综述中可以得出几个关键结论,具有直接的实践意义。首先,没有一种诊断技术适用于所有情况。诊断方法的选择应根据特定病原体(如细菌、病毒或寄生虫)、样本类型(如血液、BALF或组织)以及临床情境(如常规筛查、暴发调查或确认性诊断)来决定。第三,应进行成本效益分析,以指导实际部署决策,特别是在资源有限的环境中,先进科技可能成本过高。总之,实验室猴诊断的未来并不在于用新兴技术取代现有方法,而在于它们的战略整合。作为与人类基因关系最接近的非人灵长类动物模型,实验室猴在生命科学研究、药物开发和生物制品评估中不可或缺。然而,实验室猴群中流行的传染病或在繁殖和饲养过程中获得的传染病——例如B病毒和结核分枝杆菌——威胁着动物福利和种群安全,同时增加了人兽共患病传播的风险,并影响了研究数据的可靠性。多样性、复杂性...

title: Socioeconomic inequality in the completion of the continuum of care for maternal, newborn, and child health in Malawi

full_text: AbstractBackgroundDespite improvements in maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) service coverage in Malawi, completion of the continuum of care (CoC) remains low and unequally distributed across socioeconomic groups. This study quantified socioeconomic inequality in MNCH CoC completion and its determinants.MethodsWe analyzed pooled data from the 2010, 2015–16, and 2024 Malawi Demographic and Health Surveys, including 18,741 women with a live birth; analytic samples were 15,552 women for maternal CoC and 7,625 children aged 12–23 months for full CoC. Wealth-related inequality was assessed using Erreygers concentration indices. Multivariable and multilevel logistic regression identified determinants of CoC completion, while Wagstaff, Oaxaca–Blinder, Fairlie, and inequality-of-opportunity decompositions identified inequality contributors.ResultsFull CoC completion rose from 1.4% (2010) to 6.8% (2024); maternal CoC rose from 4.9% to 17.4%. Women completed an average of 8.3 of 11 interventions. Pro-rich inequality persisted for maternal CoC (Erreygers index = 0.036, p < 0.001); inequality in full CoC was smaller and not statistically significant (0.004, p = 0.497). Women's education, particularly higher education, was the strongest and most consistent predictor of completion (adjusted OR: 3.42 maternal, 3.45 full CoC, pooled). Contributors varied by method: education, wealth, and rural residence dominated the Wagstaff decomposition, while education, age, and parity contributed more consistently in the Oaxaca–Blinder and Fairlie decompositions. Circumstance variables reproduced the entirety of observed maternal CoC inequality, falling to 78.7% when wealth was excluded.ConclusionsAlthough MNCH CoC coverage improved substantially in Malawi, socioeconomic inequalities persisted, particularly for maternal CoC, and were closely linked to structural circumstances. Policies improving geographic access, expanding girls’ and women's education, and addressing structural barriers may support more equitable progress toward Sustainable Development Goal 3.Keywords: concentration index, continuum of care, decomposition, inequality of opportunity, Malawi, maternal health, socioeconomic inequality MethodsStudy design and data sourceThis study utilised data from the 2010, 2015–16, and 2024 Malawi Demographic and Health Surveys (MDHS), nationally representative household surveys conducted by the National Statistical Office in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and ICF through the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) Programme. The MDHS employs a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design. In the first stage, enumeration areas are selected from the national census sampling frame using probability proportional to size. In the second stage, households are systematically sampled within selected clusters. The surveys are designed to provide reliable estimates of health indicators at national, regional, and urban-rural levels. Detailed information regarding survey design and sampling procedures is available in the respective MDHS reports (27).Study populationThe study population comprised women aged 15–49 years who had a live birth within the two years preceding each Malawi Demographic and Health Survey (MDHS). Consistent with previous continuum-of-care (CoC) studies (8, 9, 28), only the most recent live birth was retained to minimise recall bias and ensure comparability across survey rounds. After restricting to the most recent live birth of a child aged under 24 months and still alive at interview, 7,356 women were retained from the 2010 survey, 6,456 from the 2015–16 survey and 4,929 from the 2024 survey. Analyses of childhood vaccination and the complete 11-component continuum of care were further restricted to children aged 12–23 months (3,660 in 2010; 3,161 in 2015–16; 2,468 in 2024). Observations with missing values on any continuum component or study covariate were then excluded under a strict complete-case rule, yielding final analytical samples of 15,552 women for the maternal continuum of care (6,901 in 2010; 5,211 in 2015–16; 3,440 in 2024) and 7,625 children for the full continuum of care (3,442 in 2010; 2,523 in 2015–16; 1,660 in 2024). These complete-case samples were used throughout the analysis; the unweighted sample size for each estimate is reported in the corresponding tables, See Figure 1.Figure 1Participant flow diagram. Complete-case restriction required non-missing values on all continuum components (early ANC4+, tetanus, facility delivery, skilled attendance, maternal PNC ≤48 h, early breastfeeding, modern contraception, and — for full CoC — BCG, DPT3, Polio3, measles) and all analytical covariates (age, parity, woman's and husband's education, residence, region, wealth, distance to facility, radio/newspaper/TV exposure). These two pooled N's (15,552 and 7,625) are the denominators used in all tables and the Abstract.Flowchart comparing sample sizes from MDHS 2010, 2015–16, and 2024 surveys, with a sequence from women interviewed to children aged twelve to twenty-three months, ending with pooled strict complete-case maternal and full CoC sample counts.Outcome variableThe primary outcome was completion of the maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) continuum of care (CoC). Because there is no universally standardized measure of the MNCH continuum of care, the outcome was constructed using the composite coverage approach described in previous studies (28, 29). The continuum comprised eleven interventions: early ANC4+ (at least four antenatal visits with the first visit before the fourth month of pregnancy), ≥2 tetanus toxoid doses, facility delivery, skilled birth attendance, maternal postnatal care within 48 h, early initiation of breastfeeding, modern contraceptive use, BCG, DPT3, Polio3 and measles vaccination. Women and children aged 12–23 months who received all eleven interventions were coded 1 (complete); otherwise 0 (incomplete). The full continuum was assessed only among children aged 12–23 months. Newborn postnatal care was excluded because the DHS item was not comparable across survey rounds. A four-contact ANC threshold, commonly used in CoC studies (28), was retained for temporal comparability across the three surveys; sensitivity analyses using ≥8 contacts were conducted for the 2024 round (Supplementary Tables S1–S3).Explanatory variablesThe explanatory variables were selected based on previous literature examining determinants of continuum of care utilisation and socioeconomic inequalities in maternal and child health service use (7, 8, 29, 30). Guided by the World Health Organization Social Determinants of Health Framework (31), Covariates were grouped into individual, household, and contextual factors. Individual-level variables included maternal age, parity, maternal educational attainment (no education, primary, secondary, and higher), and exposure to radio, television, and newspapers or magazines. Household-level variables included household wealth quintile, partner's educational attainment, and perceived distance to a health facility. Contextual factors comprised place of residence, region of residence, survey year, and the DHS primary sampling unit (PSU). Early antenatal care initiation was not included as a covariate because it is embedded in the early-ANC4+ component of the continuum-of-care outcomes.Measurement of socioeconomic inequalitySocioeconomic inequality in completion of the MNCH continuum of care was assessed using concentration curves and concentration indices (8, 9, 32). Concentration curves were constructed by plotting the cumulative proportion of continuum of care completion against the cumulative proportion of women ranked according to household wealth, beginning with the poorest and ending with the richest. A concentration curve below the line of equality indicates a pro-rich distribution, whereas a curve above the line indicates a pro-poor distribution. The standard concentration index (CI) was estimated as:CI=2μcov(yi,Ri)where μ denotes the mean of the outcome variable, yi represents continuum of care completion, and Ri is the fractional rank of the individual in the wealth distribution. Because completion of the continuum of care is a binary outcome, the Erreygers corrected concentration index (ECI) was used as the primary measure of inequality to account for the bounded nature of the variable (32). The ECI was calculated as:ECI=4μ×CIPositive values indicate that completion of the continuum of care is concentrated among wealthier women, while negative values indicate concentration among poorer women. To examine the extent to which selected socioeconomic and geographic characteristics statistically reproduce the observed wealth-related inequality in maternal continuum of care (CoC), we estimated circumstances-only logistic regression models, following an inequality-of-opportunity approach (41). The full model included household wealth, place of residence, region, and partner's education. A second model excluded household wealth in order to assess how the reproduced inequality changed when wealth was omitted. Predicted probabilities from each model were obtained, and Erreygers concentration indices were calculated on these fitted probabilities using the survey design. The percentage of observed inequality that is statistically reproduced was defined as:IOp=(CIcircumstancesCItotal)×100where CIcircumstances represents the concentration index of the predicted probabilities based on the selected circumstance variables and CItotal represents the total observed concentration index. Higher values indicate a greater proportion of the observed inequality that is statistically reproduced by the selected circumstance variables.Determinants of continuum of care completionTo identify factors associated with completion of the continuum of care, logistic regression and multilevel logistic regression models were fitted. Survey-weighted logistic regression models were estimated separately for each survey round and for the pooled sample, with survey year included in the pooled model. The models accounted for the MDHS sampling weights, PSU clustering, and survey stratification. Because women and their children were nested within DHS primary sampling units (PSUs)/enumeration areas (clusters), a two-level random-intercept logistic regression model was estimated to account for clustering and between-PSU heterogeneity. The multilevel logistic model was specified as:ln[Pij1−Pij]=β0+β1X1ij+β2X2ij+...+βkXkij+ujwhere Pij denotes the probability that woman i in cluster j completed the continuum of care, β0 is the intercept, Xkij represents the explanatory variables, βk denotes the corresponding regression coefficients, and uj represents the PSU-level random effect. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Between-PSU variation was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), calculated as:ICC=σu2σu2+π23where σ2u represents the PSU-level variance. The ICC quantifies the proportion of residual variation in completion of the continuum of care attributable to differences between PSUs.Decomposition of socioeconomic inequalityTo identify the contributions of individual determinants to wealth-related inequality in continuum of care completion, the Erreygers concentration index (ECI) was decomposed using the Wagstaff decomposition approach (33). This method decomposes the observed inequality into the contributions of individual explanatory variables based on their association with continuum of care completion and their distribution across household wealth groups. Positive contributions indicate that a variable increases pro-rich inequality, whereas negative contributions indicate that it reduces inequality. To further examine wealth-related differences in continuum of care completion, Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition was used to decompose the observed rich–poor gap into components attributable to differences in population characteristics (endowments) and differences in the effects of those characteristics (coefficients). Because continuum of care completion is a binary outcome, Fairlie decomposition was also performed. The Fairlie approach extends the Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition to nonlinear models and estimates the contribution of individual explanatory variables to the observed gap between wealth groups (34).Statistical analysisDescriptive statistics were used to summarise respondent characteristics and continuum of care completion. Concentration curves and Erreygers concentration indices were estimated to assess socioeconomic inequality. Survey-weighted logistic regression and multilevel logistic regression models were fitted to identify determinants of continuum of care completion. Wagstaff, Oaxaca–Blinder and Fairlie decompositions were conducted to identify drivers of socioeconomic inequality. All analyses accounted for the complex survey design. Within each survey round, sampling weights, primary sampling units and strata were applied as provided by DHS. After pooling, PSU and strata identifiers were made unique across rounds by grouping survey year with the original cluster and stratum codes; sampling weights were carried forward from each round without rescaling. Statistical significance was assessed at p < 0.05. Analyses were performed in Stata version 18.Ethical considerationsThe study used publicly available secondary data obtained from the DHS Programme following formal approval. Ethical approval for the original surveys was granted by the Malawi National Health Sciences Research Committee and the Institutional Review Board of ICF. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before data collection. The datasets were fully anonymised before being released for research purposes, and no personal identifiers were available to the investigators. Study design and data sourceThis study utilised data from the 2010, 2015–16, and 2024 Malawi Demographic and Health Surveys (MDHS), nationally representative household surveys conducted by the National Statistical Office in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and ICF through the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) Programme. The MDHS employs a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design. In the first stage, enumeration areas are selected from the national census sampling frame using probability proportional to size. In the second stage, households are systematically sampled within selected clusters. The surveys are designed to provide reliable estimates of health indicators at national, regional, and urban-rural levels. Detailed information regarding survey design and sampling procedures is available in the respective MDHS reports (27). Supplementary materialThe Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frph.2026.1919232/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials ResultsDescriptive statistics and coverage trendsTable 1 summarises the socio-demographic and household characteristics of women included in the three Malawi Demographic and Health Surveys. The strict complete-case sample comprised 15,552 women (6,901 in 2010; 5,211 in 2015–16; and 3,440 in 2024). Across survey rounds, the educational profile of the sample changed: the proportion of women with no formal education declined from 16.2% in 2010 to 6.2% in 2024, while the proportion with secondary or higher education increased. The distribution of residence and region remained relatively stable; overall, 85.7% of women resided in rural areas and 43.9% lived in the Southern Region. In the pooled sample, 16.1% of women received early ANC4+, defined as at least four antenatal visits with the first visit occurring before the fourth month of pregnancy. Radio exposure was reported by 56.9% of women, newspaper exposure by 19.2% and television exposure by 15.9%. Perceived distance to a health facility was reported as a big problem by 56.9% of women. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis study utilized three rounds of nationally representative DHS data (2010–2024) to examine the magnitude of socioeconomic inequality in MNCH continuum of care completion, identify the determinants of continuum of care completion, and determine the factors contributing most to observed socioeconomic inequalities. Over this period, completion of the full eleven-component continuum nearly doubled, and maternal continuum completion also rose substantially. This progress coincides with the expansion of national maternal and child health programs and community-based service delivery (27). Despite these gains, pro-rich inequality in maternal CoC completion persisted throughout the study. In contrast, inequality in the full continuum was not statistically significant in any survey round or in the pooled analysis, suggesting that broader access to the continuum was comparatively more equitable throughout the study period. However, completion of services requiring repeated contact with the health system remained socioeconomically patterned. This finding provides only partial support for the inverse equity hypothesis, which posits that newly expanded services are first adopted by wealthier groups before spreading more evenly (11).Given that overall completion of the full continuum remained modest, it is important to identify points of care discontinuation. Most women initiated contact with the health system through skilled antenatal care (ANC) and facility delivery. However, completion rates declined for repeated ANC visits, timely postnatal care, and childhood immunization. This pattern, where women initiate but do not complete the recommended package of care, has been observed by (9). This contrasts with countries like Lao PDR (35), The Gambia (36), and Ghana (37), where overall completion remained very low from the outset. In Malawi, discontinuity is concentrated in the later stages of the continuum, which may reflect the cumulative burden of repeated facility contact, competing household responsibilities, and the travel and opportunity costs associated with multiple visits (38).These determinants align with Andersen's Behavioral Model of health service use. Women's education, particularly higher education, emerged as the strongest and most consistent predictor of both maternal and full CoC completion, underscoring the pivotal role of educational attainment in sustained engagement across the continuum. More educated women may have greater opportunities to access health information, navigate the health system, and follow through on recommended contacts, health education, and referrals to other services (14, 23, 39). Perceived distance to a facility and partner's education were also independently associated with completion. The DHS measure of perceived distance captures a woman's belief that reaching a facility is problematic, rather than actual travel distance. This likely reflects a combination of physical accessibility, transport availability, cost, and prior experience with the referral system, rather than distance alone. This is consistent with evidence on referral delays and transport constraints within Malawi's rural health system (38, 40). These findings align with the WHO Social Determinants of Health framework, which identifies education, wealth, and geographic access as fundamental influences on health opportunity (31). The inequality-of-opportunity analysis further reinforced this structural interpretation: circumstance variables (household wealth, residence, region, and partner's education) statistically reproduced the entirety of the observed pro-rich inequality in maternal CoC completion, falling to 78.7% when wealth was excluded. Given the observational, cross-sectional design, this indicates that observed inequality is closely associated with the selected socioeconomic and contextual circumstance variables, an interpretation broadly consistent with Roemer's Equality of Opportunity framework (41). This implies that reducing inequality will necessitate structural interventions alongside behavior-change strategies.Across the three decomposition methods, women's and partner's education emerged as a relatively consistent contributor to wealth-related inequality, whereas radio exposure and perceived distance to a health facility contributed strongly in the Wagstaff decomposition but far less, and often non-significantly, in the Fairlie decomposition. Because the three methods decompose different aspects of inequality, the concentration index, the mean gap, and its non-linear counterpart, these results should be read as complementary rather than mutually confirming, and areas of divergence, such as those for radio exposure and perceived distance, are as informative as areas of convergence. This refines earlier Malawian evidence that identified geographical region as the largest single contributor (8), suggesting that regional disparities may partly reflect underlying differences in education, access to information, and practical barriers to care rather than geography per se (38, 40). The multilevel analysis further indicated that, although modest, cluster-level (PSU-level) variation in CoC completion persisted even after accounting for individual and household characteristics. This suggests an independent role for unmeasured contextual factors such as service availability, staffing, and local norms surrounding maternal healthcare. Collectively, these findings support strengthening community health worker programs and mobile outreach in underserved areas, expanding girls’ and women's education, and encouraging male involvement in maternal healthcare (24), particularly given that most of the observed wealth-related inequality in maternal CoC completion was statistically reproduced by circumstance variables such as wealth, residence, region, and partner's education.Policy implicationsBased on the findings improving completion of the continuum of care in Malawi may require attention to both individual- and contextual-level barriers to maternal and child health service utilisation, in line with priorities already reflected in Malawi's Health Sector Strategic Plan. Given the strength and consistency of the association between women's education and CoC completion, continued investment in girls’ education and in demand-generation strategies that reach less-educated women, including community health worker outreach and mobile/outreach clinics in underserved areas, may be a productive entry point. The independent association of partner's education with completion, together with existing qualitative evidence on the benefits of male engagement in maternal healthcare, supports continued efforts to involve male partners in antenatal and postnatal care rather than treating maternal health as a woman-only concern. The persistent association between perceived distance and completion, alongside modest but persistent cluster-level variation, points to a continued role for improving geographic and financial access to services for women from poorer and rural households and for addressing local supply-side differences in service delivery. Reducing socioeconomic inequality in CoC completion is therefore likely to require a combination of demand-side interventions (education, male engagement, information and outreach) and supply-side and structural measures (facility access, service quality, and household-level poverty reduction) rather than either alone.LimitationsThis study has several limitations. First, the analysis relied on self-reported DHS data, which may be subject to recall and social desirability bias. Second, the cross-sectional design precludes establishing causal relationships between the explanatory variables and continuum of care completion. Third, the DHS does not capture supply-side factors, such as health facility readiness and quality of care, which may influence completion of the continuum of care. Fourth, the DHS measure of perceived di…
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionThis study examined socioeconomic inequality in the completion of the eleven-component maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) continuum of care in Malawi using three rounds of nationally representative Demographic and Health Survey data. Although completion of the continuum of care improved over the study period, pro-rich socioeconomic inequality remained. Women's education, particularly higher education, was consistently associated with higher completion of both the maternal and full continuum of care, while partner's education and perceived distance to a health facility remained important correlates of completion. The findings further suggest that much of the observed wealth-related inequality in continuum of care completion is associated with socioeconomic and contextual circumstances, underscoring the persistent in8uence of structural disadvantage.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionDespite substantial progress in reducing maternal and child mortality over recent decades, maternal, new-born, and child health (MNCH) remains a major public health challenge globally, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Between 2000 and 2020, the global maternal mortality ratio declined considerably; however, SSA still accounts for nearly 70% of maternal deaths worldwide (1). Similarly, although neonatal mortality has decreased over time, the pace of reduction remains insufficient to achieve Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets by 2030 (2). Malawi continues to face a significant burden of maternal and child mortality despite notable improvements in access to essential health services, highlighting the need for strategies that strengthen maternal and child survival across the entire reproductive and early childhood period (3, 4).The continuum of care (CoC) framework has emerged as a cornerstone of maternal and child health programming because it promotes the delivery of integrated interventions from pregnancy through childbirth, the postnatal period, and early childhood (5). The framework emphasises that maternal and child health outcomes are maximised when women and children receive a complete package of services, including antenatal care, skilled birth attendance, postnatal care, immunisation, breastfeeding support, and family planning. Evidence from a recent systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated that completion of the continuum of care significantly reduces maternal and neonatal mortality, while discontinuity at any stage increases the risk of adverse outcomes (5). Nevertheless, completion of the continuum remains low across many low- and middle-income countries. A pooled analysis of sub-Saharan African countries estimated that only 36% of women completed the maternal continuum of care (6), while a systematic review of African studies reported an average completion rate of only 20.9% (7).Beyond low coverage, evidence increasingly shows that utilisation of continuum of care services is unequally distributed across socioeconomic groups. Multi-country studies conducted in SSA have consistently reported pro-rich inequalities in continuum of care completion, with women from wealthier households being substantially more likely to complete maternal health services than women from poorer households (8, 9). Similar patterns have been documented in Bangladesh, Ethiopia, and other low- and middle-income countries, where wealth, education, residence, and access to information strongly influence progression through the continuum of care (10–13). Studies further suggest that socioeconomic disadvantages accumulate across successive stages of care, leading to widening inequalities as women progress from antenatal care to delivery, postnatal care, and child health services (14, 15).In Malawi, socioeconomic inequalities have been documented across several health outcomes and services, including HIV knowledge, cervical cancer screening, maternal healthcare utilisation, and childhood immunisation (16–21). Evidence also indicates persistent disparities in antenatal care utilisation and postnatal care uptake (22–26). However, most existing studies focus on individual maternal or child health interventions rather than continuity across the full maternal, newborn, and child health pathway. Furthermore, while regional studies have examined wealth-related inequalities in continuum of care completion, Malawi remains underrepresented in country-specific analyses investigating the magnitude and underlying drivers of socioeconomic inequality across the complete continuum of care (8, 9).Understanding the extent and determinants of socioeconomic inequality in continuum of care completion is essential for designing equitable policies aimed at improving maternal and child health outcomes and achieving Universal Health Coverage. Although previous studies have identified factors associated with continuum of care utilisation, limited evidence exists on the drivers contributing to wealth-related inequalities in completion of the full maternal, newborn, and child health continuum of care in Malawi. This study addresses this gap by examining socioeconomic inequality in the completion of an eleven-component MNCH continuum of care using nationally representative data from the 2010, 2015–16, and 2024 Malawi Demographic and Health Surveys. Specifically, the study aimed to: (1) measure socioeconomic inequality and its severity in the completion of the continuum of care; (2) identify determinants of continuum of care completion; and (3) determine the factors contributing most to observed socioeconomic inequalities. Study populationThe study population comprised women aged 15–49 years who had a live birth within the two years preceding each Malawi Demographic and Health Survey (MDHS). Consistent with previous continuum-of-care (CoC) studies (8, 9, 28), only the most recent live birth was retained to minimise recall bias and ensure comparability across survey rounds. After restricting to the most recent live birth of a child aged under 24 months and still alive at interview, 7,356 women were retained from the 2010 survey, 6,456 from the 2015–16 survey and 4,929 from the 2024 survey. Analyses of childhood vaccination and the complete 11-component continuum of care were further restricted to children aged 12–23 months (3,660 in 2010; 3,161 in 2015–16; 2,468 in 2024). Observations with missing values on any continuum component or study covariate were then excluded under a strict complete-case rule, yielding final analytical samples of 15,552 women for the maternal continuum of care (6,901 in 2010; 5,211 in 2015–16; 3,440 in 2024) and 7,625 children for the full continuum of care (3,442 in 2010; 2,523 in 2015–16; 1,660 in 2024). These complete-case samples were used throughout the analysis; the unweighted sample size for each estimate is reported in the corresponding tables, See Figure 1.Figure 1Participant flow diagram. Complete-case restriction required non-missing values on all continuum components (early ANC4+, tetanus, facility delivery, skilled attendance, maternal PNC ≤48 h, early breastfeeding, modern contraception, and — for full CoC — BCG, DPT3, Polio3, measles) and all analytical covariates (age, parity, woman's and husband's education, residence, region, wealth, distance to facility, radio/newspaper/TV exposure). Outcome variableThe primary outcome was completion of the maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) continuum of care (CoC). Because there is no universally standardized measure of the MNCH continuum of care, the outcome was constructed using the composite coverage approach described in previous studies (28, 29). The continuum comprised eleven interventions: early ANC4+ (at least four antenatal visits with the first visit before the fourth month of pregnancy), ≥2 tetanus toxoid doses, facility delivery, skilled birth attendance, maternal postnatal care within 48 h, early initiation of breastfeeding, modern contraceptive use, BCG, DPT3, Polio3 and measles vaccination. Women and children aged 12–23 months who received all eleven interventions were coded 1 (complete); otherwise 0 (incomplete). The full continuum was assessed only among children aged 12–23 months. Newborn postnatal care was excluded because the DHS item was not comparable across survey rounds. A four-contact ANC threshold, commonly used in CoC studies (28), was retained for temporal comparability across the three surveys; sensitivity analyses using ≥8 contacts were conducted for the 2024 round (Supplementary Tables S1–S3). title: Oncolytic virotherapy for cancer: biological mechanisms, clinical advances, and future perspectives
abstract: Abstract Oncolytic virotherapy has emerged as a promising cancer treatment that combines selective tumor destruction with potent stimulation of antitumor immunity. Unlike conventional therapies, oncolytic viruses (OVs) preferentially infect and replicate within malignant cells while sparing normal tissues, leading to direct tumor lysis and the release of tumor-associated antigens, pathogen-associated molecular patterns, and damage-associated molecular patterns that activate both innate and adaptive immune responses. Advances in molecular virology and genetic engineering have transformed naturally occurring viruses into programmable therapeutic platforms capable of delivering immunomodulatory payloads that enhance antitumor efficacy and remodel the tumor microenvironment. Multiple DNA- and RNA-based viral platforms, including herpes simplex virus, adenovirus, vaccinia virus, reovirus, measles virus, Newcastle disease virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, and coxsackievirus, are currently under clinical investigation, with regulatory approval of talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) and G47Δ providing important proof of clinical feasibility. Increasing evidence indicates that OVs can convert immunologically "cold" tumors into "hot" tumors, thereby improving responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors and other therapeutic modalities. Consequently, oncolytic virotherapy has become an attractive component of combination strategies involving immunotherapy, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapies, and cellular therapies. Nevertheless, several challenges continue to limit its broader clinical application, including antiviral immune clearance, inefficient systemic delivery, restricted intratumoral spread, tumor heterogeneity, manufacturing complexity, and the lack of robust predictive biomarkers. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the biological foundations of oncolytic virotherapy, viral engineering strategies, mechanisms of tumor selectivity, direct oncolysis, immunogenic cell death, and immune remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. It further summarizes the major oncolytic virus platforms, recent preclinical and clinical advances, emerging combination strategies, current translational challenges, and future directions expected to advance precision oncolytic virotherapy and expand its role in modern cancer treatment. Graphical Abstract Comprehensive overview of oncolytic virotherapy (OVT) from fundamental biology to clinical translation Introduction Cancer remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide despite remarkable advances in diagnosis and treatment [1]. According to recent global estimates, nearly 20 million new cancer cases and approximately 10 million cancer-related deaths occur annually, and these numbers are expected to increase substantially over the coming decades owing to population aging and continued demographic growth [2]. Although improvements in screening, surgery, radiotherapy, systemic chemotherapy, targeted therapies, and immunotherapy have significantly improved patient outcomes in several malignancies, durable disease control remains elusive for many patients with advanced or metastatic cancer [3, 4]. Tumor heterogeneity, therapeutic resistance, immune evasion, and treatment-associated toxicities continue to limit the long-term effectiveness of current therapeutic strategies, highlighting the urgent need for more selective and durable anticancer approaches [5, 6]. Among recent advances in cancer therapy, immunotherapy has fundamentally changed the treatment landscape by harnessing the patient's immune system to recognize and eliminate malignant cells [7]. Immune checkpoint inhibitors, adoptive cell therapies, and cancer vaccines have produced remarkable and durable responses in selected patient populations. However, the clinical benefits of these approaches remain restricted to a subset of patients because many tumors possess an immunosuppressive microenvironment characterized by poor immune-cell infiltration, impaired antigen presentation, and multiple mechanisms of immune escape. These so-called "cold" tumors often respond poorly to existing immunotherapies, emphasizing the need for therapeutic strategies capable of simultaneously destroying tumor cells and stimulating effective antitumor immunity [8,9,10]. Oncolytic virotherapy has emerged as one of the most promising immunotherapeutic platforms to address these challenges [11]. Unlike conventional anticancer therapies that primarily target tumor cell proliferation or specific oncogenic pathways, oncolytic viruses (OVs) selectively infect, replicate within, and lyse malignant cells while largely sparing normal tissues. Viral replication within tumors not only induces direct cancer cell destruction but also initiates a cascade of immunological events that convert dying tumors into highly immunogenic sites. The release of tumor-associated antigens together with pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) promotes dendritic-cell activation, antigen presentation, and the subsequent induction of both innate and adaptive antitumor immune responses. Consequently, OVs function as dual-action therapeutics that combine direct oncolysis with immune-mediated tumor eradication [11, 12]. The concept of using viruses to treat cancer originated more than a century ago following observations that some patients experienced transient tumor regression after naturally acquired viral infections [13]. However, the clinical application of this concept remained limited until advances in molecular virology and genetic engineering enabled the development of viruses with enhanced tumor selectivity, improved safety, and greater therapeutic efficacy. These technological advances transformed naturally occurring viruses into programmable therapeutic platforms capable of delivering immunostimulatory molecules, cytokines, checkpoint inhibitors, tumor suppressors, and other therapeutic payloads directly to the tumor microenvironment [14,15,16]. Today, oncolytic virotherapy represents a rapidly evolving field at the intersection of virology, immunology, genetic engineering, and precision oncology [11]. A wide variety of DNA and RNA viruses have been developed as oncolytic platforms, including herpes simplex virus, adenovirus, vaccinia virus, reovirus, measles virus, Newcastle disease virus, vesicular stomatitis virus, and coxsackievirus. Each platform possesses distinct biological characteristics that influence tumor selectivity, genome engineering capacity, immune activation, and delivery strategies [17, 18, 19]. Among these, genetically modified herpes simplex virus has achieved the greatest clinical success, culminating in regulatory approval of talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) for advanced melanoma and G47Δ for malignant glioma in Japan. These milestones have provided important clinical proof of concept that engineered viruses can be translated into effective cancer therapeutics [20, 21]. Increasing evidence now indicates that the therapeutic activity of OVs extends far beyond direct tumor lysis. Viral infection remodels the tumor microenvironment by promoting immune-cell recruitment, enhancing antigen presentation, stimulating inflammatory cytokine production, and reversing local immunosuppression [11, 22, 23]. Through these mechanisms, OVs can convert immunologically "cold" tumors into "hot" tumors that are more responsive to immune checkpoint blockade and other immunotherapies. This ability has positioned oncolytic virotherapy as an attractive partner for combination treatment strategies involving immune checkpoint inhibitors, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapies, cellular immunotherapies, and emerging precision medicine approaches [11, 16, 18]. Despite substantial progress, several important challenges continue to limit the widespread clinical implementation of oncolytic virotherapy. Host antiviral immunity can rapidly neutralize therapeutic viruses following systemic administration, reducing tumor delivery and persistence. In addition, the dense extracellular matrix, abnormal tumor vasculature, and highly heterogeneous tumor microenvironment can restrict viral dissemination within solid tumors [24, 25]. Manufacturing complexity, biomarker identification, optimal patient selection, and the design of effective combination regimens also remain major obstacles to broader clinical translation [26, 27]. Consequently, improving viral engineering, developing innovative delivery systems, identifying predictive biomarkers, and optimizing rational combination therapies have become major priorities in the next generation of OV research [27, 28]. Collectively, these advances have shifted the perception of oncolytic viruses from simple tumor-lytic agents to multifunctional immunotherapeutic platforms capable of integrating direct cytotoxicity with immune modulation. Rather than serving solely as stand-alone therapies, OVs are increasingly viewed as versatile components of multimodal cancer treatment designed to enhance the efficacy of existing therapeutic modalities while overcoming resistance mechanisms [11, 29]. In this review article, we provide a comprehensive overview of the biological principles underlying oncolytic virotherapy, including viral engineering strategies, mechanisms of tumor selectivity, direct oncolysis, immunogenic cell death, and immune remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. We further discuss the major oncolytic virus platforms, summarize current preclinical and clinical advances, evaluate combination strategies with established cancer therapies, examine the principal biological and translational challenges facing the field, and highlight emerging technologies that are expected to shape the next generation of precision oncolytic virotherapy. Principles and Mechanisms of Oncolytic Virotherapy Oncolytic virotherapy is based on the ability of selected viruses to preferentially infect, replicate within, and destroy cancer cells while sparing most normal tissues. Unlike conventional anticancer therapies that primarily induce direct cytotoxicity, oncolytic viruses (OVs) exert their therapeutic effects through two complementary mechanisms. First, they selectively replicate in malignant cells, leading to direct tumor destruction. Second, viral infection transforms the tumor into an inflammatory microenvironment that stimulates innate and adaptive immune responses against the cancer. Consequently, the therapeutic efficacy of modern oncolytic virotherapy depends not only on efficient viral replication but also on the generation of durable systemic antitumor immunity [28, 30,31,32,33,34]. Current evidence supports a unified mechanistic model in which therapeutic activity proceeds through sequential but interconnected events. Initially, OVs selectively target susceptible tumor cells and establish productive viral replication. This replication results in direct tumor cell lysis and the release of newly generated viral particles, enabling infection to spread throughout the tumor. Simultaneously, dying cancer cells release tumor-associated antigens (TAAs), pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), cytokines, and chemokines. Together, these molecules activate innate immune cells, promote antigen presentation, and stimulate tumor-specific T-cell responses that extend antitumor activity beyond the sites of viral infection. Thus, contemporary oncolytic virotherapy is increasingly recognized as both a targeted cytotoxic therapy and an in situ cancer vaccination strategy [30, 33, 35]. Selective Tumor Targeting (Viral Tropism) Selective tumor targeting represents the fundamental principle underlying oncolytic virotherapy. Successful treatment requires viruses to infect and replicate preferentially within malignant cells while minimizing infection of healthy tissues. This selectivity results from a combination of natural viral tropism, cancer-associated cellular abnormalities, characteristics of the tumor microenvironment, and genetic engineering approaches that further enhance tumor specificity [30, 34, 36, 37]. Natural viral tropism Natural viral tropism refers to the inherent preference of a virus for specific cell types based on the interaction between viral surface proteins and host-cell receptors. Many cancers overexpress receptors that facilitate viral attachment and entry, making malignant cells more susceptible to infection than normal tissues [11, 38]. Several clinically important OVs exploit these receptor differences. Adenovirus serotype 5 primarily enters cells through the coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor (CAR), whereas alternative adenoviral serotypes and chimeric vectors, including Ad3 and Ad5/35, preferentially utilize CD46 or desmoglein-2 (DSG2), thereby broadening their infectivity across different tumor types [16, 37, 39]. Measles virus targets CD46 and signaling lymphocytic activation molecule (SLAM), both of which are frequently upregulated in malignant tissues. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) enters cells through herpesvirus entry mediator (HVEM) and nectin-1 or nectin-2 receptors, whereas poliovirus selectively infects cells expressing CD155, a receptor that is highly expressed in numerous solid tumors and hematological malignancies [11, 18, 40]. Similarly, coxsackievirus A11 preferentially infects thoracic malignancies through intercellular adhesion molecule−1 (ICAM-1), illustrating how receptor expression can determine tumor susceptibility to specific viral platforms [41]. Although receptor abundance strongly influences viral entry, receptor expression alone does not determine therapeutic success. Productive infection also depends on the ability of tumor cells to support efficient viral replication after viral entry [11, 42]. Intracellular permissiveness Following entry into the cell, OVs rely on the intracellular environment to complete their replication cycle (Fig. 1). Cancer cells frequently harbor genetic and signaling abnormalities that unintentionally create conditions favorable for viral replication while weakening antiviral defense mechanisms [11, 43]. Activation of oncogenic pathways, including Ras, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), Wnt/β-catenin, phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT, and defects in the p53, retinoblastoma (RB)/E2F, ATM, and apoptotic signaling pathways, supports viral replication by increasing cellular metabolic activity, promoting protein synthesis, and reducing antiviral responses [11, 36, 40]. Consequently, malignant cells become substantially more permissive to viral infection than normal cells. Reovirus provides one of the best-characterized examples of this mechanism. In tumors with activated Ras signaling, antiviral protein kinase R (PKR) activity is suppressed, allowing efficient viral protein translation and replication. At the same time, Ras activation reduces type I interferon-mediated antiviral responses, enabling selective viral propagation within malignant cells while normal tissues retain effective antiviral protection [17, 18]. Similarly, many tumors exhibit defects in innate immune sensing pathways, particularly the cyclic GMP–AMP synthase–stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS–STING) pathway and type I interferon signaling. These defects impair the ability of cancer cells to detect and eliminate viral infection, thereby providing a permissive environment for OV replication. In contrast, healthy tissues generally preserve intact antiviral signaling, limiting viral replication and contributing to the favorable safety profile of many clinically developed OVs [30, 44, 45]. Influence of the tumor microenvironment The tumor microenvironment (TME) further contributes to selective viral targeting. Unlike normal tissues, solid tumors are characterized by hypoxia, abnormal vascular architecture, nutrient deprivation, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation. These conditions alter cellular metabolism and gene expression, creating an environment that often favors viral replication [33, 46]. Hypoxia is particularly important because activation of hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1) signaling promotes transcriptional programs that enhance viral gene expression and replication in several OV platforms. In addition, impaired immune surveillance within many tumors reduces early viral clearance, allowing viruses to spread more efficiently through malignant tissue than through healthy organs [36, 45]. Consequently, both intrinsic cellular defects and unique microenvironmental conditions cooperate to enhance tumor-selective viral replication. Engineering strategies to improve tumor selectivity Although many OVs possess inherent tumor selectivity, modern virotherapy increasingly relies on genetic engineering to improve specificity, maximize therapeutic efficacy, and reduce off-target toxicity (Table 1). These modifications have transformed naturally occurring viruses into highly programmable therapeutic platforms [16, 17]. Receptor retargeting modifies viral attachment proteins to redirect viral entry toward receptors that are preferentially expressed on tumor cells. Examples include adenoviral vectors engineered to utilize CD46 instead of CAR and HSV-1 vectors retargeted toward epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) or nectin-1, thereby improving infection of tumors with limited susceptibility to their native viruses [18, 40]. Transcriptional targeting restricts viral gene expression to malignant cells by placing essential viral genes under the control of tumor-selective promoters, such as those derived from human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) or survivin. Because these promoters exhibit minimal activity in most normal tissues, viral replication remains largely confined to cancer cells, thereby enhancing safety [47, 48]. analysis.summary_en: This review explores the potential of oncolytic virotherapy, particularly using measles virus, as a promising cancer treatment. It highlights the biological mechanisms of oncolytic viruses, their ability to stimulate antitumor immunity, and their role in converting immunologically cold tumors into hot ones. The review also discusses the clinical advances, including the approval of T-VEC and G47Δ, and the challenges such as immune clearance and manufacturing complexity. It emphasizes the importance of measles virus in combination strategies with immunotherapy, chemotherapy, and other modalities. The review concludes with future directions aimed at improving precision and expanding the use of oncolytic virotherapy in cancer treatment.

abstract_zh: 摘要 肿瘤溶细胞病毒治疗(OVT)作为一种结合选择性肿瘤破坏与强效抗肿瘤免疫刺激的癌症治疗方式,展现出巨大的前景。与传统疗法不同,溶细胞病毒(OVs)能够选择性地感染并复制于恶性细胞中,同时避免对正常组织的损害,从而直接导致肿瘤裂解,并释放肿瘤相关抗原、病原体相关分子模式以及损伤相关分子模式,激活先天性和适应性免疫应答。分子病毒学和基因工程领域的进展,已将天然病毒转化为可编程的治疗平台,能够递送免疫调节性载荷,增强抗肿瘤效果并重塑肿瘤微环境。目前,多种基于DNA和RNA的病毒平台,包括单纯疱疹病毒、腺病毒、牛痘病毒、轮状病毒、麻疹病毒、新城疫病毒、水疱性口炎病毒以及柯萨奇病毒,均在临床研究中,其中talimogene laherparepvec(T-VEC)和G47Δ的监管批准为临床可行性提供了重要证据。越来越多的证据表明,OVs能够将免疫学上“冷”的肿瘤转化为“热”肿瘤,从而提高其对免疫检查点抑制剂及其他治疗方式的响应性。因此,溶细胞病毒治疗已成为结合免疫治疗、化疗、放疗、靶向治疗和细胞治疗等综合策略中的一个有吸引力的组成部分。然而,一些挑战仍然限制了其更广泛的应用,包括抗病毒药物免疫清除、系统性递送效率低下、肿瘤内扩散受限、肿瘤异质性、制造复杂性以及缺乏可靠的预测性生物标志物。本综述全面概述了溶细胞病毒治疗的生物基础,包括病毒工程策略、肿瘤选择性机制、直接溶细胞作用、免疫源性细胞死亡以及肿瘤微环境的免疫重塑。此外,还总结了主要的溶细胞病毒平台、近期的临床前和临床进展、新兴的联合治疗策略、当前的转化挑战以及未来方向,旨在推动精准溶细胞病毒治疗的发展,并拓展其在现代癌症治疗中的作用。图形摘要 溶细胞病毒治疗(OVT)从基础生物学到临床转化的全面概述

title: Artificial Intelligence in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology
