full_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing healthcare, with growing relevance in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology. This review summarizes current applications of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) in these areas while critically evaluating their strengths and limitations. Although AI has shown promising performance in image analysis, molecular diagnostics, risk prediction, and clinical decision support, its routine implementation remains constrained by limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets, algorithmic bias, and challenges in generalizability and explainability. The review also discusses AI’s emerging role in scientific writing and the ethical and practical considerations associated with its clinical adoption. Overall, current evidence suggests that AI should be regarded as a complementary decision-support technology whose safe and effective integration depends on rigorous validation, high-quality data, and appropriate clinical oversight. The Dawn of Artificial Intelligence in HealthcareArtificial intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science that develops computational systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence, including pattern recognition, prediction, and decision support. Artificial intelligence has become increasingly integrated into healthcare, offering new opportunities to improve diagnostics, prognostic assessment, and clinical decision-making. Recent advances in machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs), together with the increasing availability of digital health data, have accelerated the development of AI applications across medicine (1).In infectious diseases and clinical microbiology (IDCM), AI has attracted growing interest because it can improve laboratory diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, prognostic assessment, outbreak surveillance, and clinical decision support. Although numerous studies have reported promising results, important challenges related to external validation, data quality, model generalizability, and clinical implementation continue to limit the routine adoption of these technologies.This review was prepared based on the thematic discussions, expert presentations, and literature evaluations conducted within the 2025 Basic Education Program of the Assistants and Young Specialists Commission of the Turkish Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases, entitled AI in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology. Building on these educational activities, this review critically synthesizes current evidence on AI applications in IDCM, highlighting both their clinical potential and the methodological, practical, and ethical challenges that must be addressed before widespread implementation. The Role of AI in MedicineAI in medicine has evolved from early rule-based expert systems to modern ML and DL models capable of analyzing complex clinical data (2, 3). These approaches have been widely adopted in specialties such as radiology and pathology, where image-based analysis has demonstrated substantial clinical utility (4, 5). In contrast, AI applications in IDCM remain at an earlier stage of implementation because they require integrating microbiological, clinical, and epidemiological information. Accordingly, AI systems in this field should be evaluated according to their specific clinical applications, evidence base, and limitations rather than as a single technology. ML and DL in Infectious Diseases and Clinical MicrobiologyMachine learning and DL applications in IDCM have expanded rapidly over the past decade, driven by advances in computational methods and the increasing availability of digital laboratory and clinical data. Current applications can be broadly categorized into four major areas: diagnostic automation, clinical decision support, clinical documentation and symptom assessment, and epidemiological surveillance (Table 1). Although numerous studies have demonstrated promising results, most AI systems remain task-specific and have not yet undergone sufficient prospective or multicenter validation for routine clinical implementation.Table 1.Classification of general clinical AI tools relevant to IDCM practice. Category Representative tools and systems Clinical application in infectious diseases CDSSIBM Watson (Merative), Isabel Healthcare, DXplain, VisualDx, Sepsis Watch, Bayesian HealthDifferential diagnosis of rare conditions, sepsis risk prediction, and providing actionable clinical guidance.Symptom analyzersAda Health, Symptoma, Infermedica, Healthily, DxGPT (GPT-4)Analysis of patient-reported symptoms for triage, rare disease identification, and mobile health integration.Documentation and EHR systemsSuki AI, Nabla, Nuance DAX, DeepScribe, Epic Systems, Oracle CernerAutomated clinical note generation, ICD-10 coding, sepsis monitoring, and complication prediction within EHRs.Dermatological diagnosticsSkinive.MD, VisualDxClassification of exanthematous lesions (e.g., mpox, varicella, measles) using CNNs.Molecular and genomic AIDeepARG, PathoFact, PARGT, Nextstrain, PangolinAMR gene prediction and real-time viral mutation visualization for epidemiological surveillance.AI: Artificial intelligence, AMR: Antimicrobial resistance, CNNs: Convolutional neural networks, CDSS: Clinical decision support systems, EHRs: Electronic health records, ICD-10: International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision. Diagnostic Automation and Molecular Analysis Diagnostic microbiology is among the most suitable areas for AI implementation because many laboratory procedures involve repetitive image interpretation and pattern-recognition tasks. Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have demonstrated high diagnostic performance in automated Gram stain interpretation and digital culture plate analysis, with reported agreement rates exceeding 95% under controlled experimental conditions (6). Nevertheless, further validation in diverse laboratory settings is required before widespread implementation.Artificial intelligence has also advanced molecular diagnostics through automated analysis of whole-genome sequencing data. ML-based platforms, such as DeepARG and PARGT, enable rapid identification of antimicrobial resistance genes and facilitate genomic surveillance (7, 8). However, their performance remains dependent on sequencing quality, reference database completeness, and the continuous updating of resistance gene repositories. Clinical Decision Support Systems Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) integrate laboratory findings with clinical information to assist with diagnosis, risk prediction, and treatment decisions. AI-based sepsis prediction models, including Sepsis Watch and the Epic Sepsis Prediction Model (Epic Systems, Verona, WI, USA) and Epic’s Sepsis Prediction Model, have demonstrated the potential to identify patients at increased risk before clinical deterioration occurs (9). However, inconsistent performance across institutions, false-positive alerts, and alert fatigue remain important barriers to routine implementation.Similarly, AI-assisted diagnostic support platforms combine clinical findings with large medical knowledge bases to facilitate differential diagnosis, whereas natural language processing (NLP)-based applications improve access to evidence-based recommendations and clinical guidelines (10, 11). Although these tools may improve efficiency, they should be regarded as supportive technologies rather than autonomous diagnostic systems. Symptom Analyzers, Triage, and Documentation Recent advances in NLP and LLMs have expanded AI applications to symptom assessment and clinical documentation. Symptom analyzers may assist with preliminary patient triage, whereas AI-powered documentation systems can automatically generate clinical notes and reduce administrative workload (12-15). Despite these advantages, current LLM-based applications remain susceptible to hallucinations, incomplete contextual understanding, and variable performance across different clinical scenarios, emphasizing the need for careful clinician review. Epidemiological Surveillance and Real-World Performance Artificial intelligence has become an increasingly valuable tool for infectious disease surveillance by supporting genomic epidemiology, outbreak monitoring, and pathogen evolution analysis. Platforms such as Nextstrain have played an important role in monitoring viral evolution during the COVID-19 pandemic (16, 17). At the same time, the pandemic highlighted the importance of representative datasets, continuous model updating, and external validation, demonstrating that algorithmic performance alone does not guarantee successful implementation in real-world public health settings (18-20). From Microscope to AI: Current Evidence on AI Models in Medical ParasitologyMicroscopic diagnosis remains the cornerstone of medical parasitology but is often labor-intensive and dependent on experienced personnel. Consequently, AI-based image analysis has emerged as a promising approach to improve diagnostic efficiency and standardization, particularly in settings with limited access to expert microscopists (21).Current evidence is strongest for blood-borne parasites, particularly Plasmodium spp., where CNN-based models have consistently demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy under experimental conditions (22, 23). Similar automated ML frameworks are being developed to identify intestinal parasites in stool samples. For instance, DL algorithms trained on large datasets of helminth eggs have shown significant potential to differentiate species with high morphological similarity, such as Ascaris lumbricoides and Trichuris trichiura (24).More recently, multimodal LLMs, including GPT-4 and Gemini, have been explored for parasitological image interpretation. However, unlike CNN-based models specifically trained for image classification, these general-purpose systems have shown inconsistent performance in recognizing complex microscopic structures and remain susceptible to hallucinations, particularly when image quality or contextual information is limited (25).Recent literature largely agrees that while advanced computational models offer promising support for education and second-opinion assessment, they cannot yet function as primary diagnostic tools in parasitology. Therefore, current evidence supports using AI as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, expert microscopic evaluation, particularly in diagnostically challenging cases (26). DL in the Diagnosis of Exanthematous Infectious DiseasesDeep learning has been increasingly investigated for automated recognition of infectious skin diseases because visual lesion assessment is an important component of clinical diagnosis. Most studies have focused on CNN-based image classification models that can distinguish common exanthematous infections from non-infectious skin disorders (27, 28).Recent studies have explored CNN-based models for classifying infectious skin diseases, including mpox, Lyme disease, and measles (29-32). While these studies report promising diagnostic performance in controlled experimental settings, their generalizability to real-world clinical environments remains uncertain and requires further validation (33).Deep learning-supported systems also hold potential in dermatology by improving diagnostic consistency in atypical presentations and supporting remote evaluation through teledermatology applications (34). However, these systems’ performance depends heavily on the quality, representativeness, and diversity of training datasets. A major limitation is algorithmic bias, particularly the underrepresentation of darker skin tones in publicly available datasets, which may reduce diagnostic accuracy across diverse populations (35, 36).In addition, many current DL models rely exclusively on visual inputs and do not incorporate critical clinical information such as associated symptoms (e.g., fever, pruritus) or disease course, which are essential for differentiating infectious exanthems from non-infectious conditions such as drug eruptions.Several commercially available mobile applications provide AI-assisted assessment of skin lesions; however, they should be regarded as screening tools rather than diagnostic systems because performance varies by image quality, lesion characteristics, and patient population (35, 36).Future research should prioritize prospective multicenter validation and the integration of clinical, epidemiological, and imaging data to improve the robustness and clinical applicability of AI models for infectious skin diseases. AI-Based Antimicrobial ManagementAntimicrobial stewardship (AMS) is one of the most promising applications of AI in infectious diseases because it requires the integration of microbiological, clinical, and epidemiological data to support timely treatment decisions. Current AI applications focus primarily on optimizing empirical antibiotic selection, identifying patients at increased risk of resistant infections, and supporting antimicrobial prescribing through CDSS (37, 38).ML models, particularly those analyzing longitudinal electronic health record data, have demonstrated encouraging performance in predicting healthcare-associated infections and identifying patients at high risk of multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO) infections, including carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) (39, 40). These models may enable earlier risk stratification than conventional clinical scoring systems and support more targeted empirical antimicrobial therapy. However, most available evidence originates from retrospective studies, and prospective validation across different healthcare settings remains limited.Although DL models can identify complex relationships within large clinical datasets, their predictions are often difficult to interpret in routine clinical practice. Explainable AI (XAI) approaches may help clinicians understand which variables contribute most to model predictions and thereby improve confidence in AI-assisted recommendations. However, XAI does not provide complete transparency into the internal processes of complex models and should not be interpreted as establishing causal relationships (41-43).Large language models have recently emerged as potential AMS tools by summarizing clinical guidelines, assisting with literature retrieval, and supporting educational activities. Nevertheless, current LLMs remain susceptible to hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and limited access to real-time patient-specific information, limiting their use for independent therapeutic decision-making (44, 45).Overall, current evidence suggests that AI has considerable potential to optimize AMS by improving risk prediction and supporting antimicrobial prescribing. However, despite encouraging predictive performance, robust evidence demonstrating improvements in prescribing quality, antimicrobial consumption, or patient outcomes remains limited. Future progress will depend on high-quality clinical data, rigorous external validation, and successful integration of AI tools into AMS programs and routine clinical workflows (46). ML Applications in Predicting the Prognosis of Infectious DiseasesPredicting disease progression is one of the most promising AI applications in infectious diseases because timely risk stratification can improve patient management and resource allocation. Unlike diagnostic models, prognostic models aim to estimate future clinical outcomes by integrating clinical, laboratory, and increasingly multi-omics data. Recent advances in multi-omics technologies have enabled the integration of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and conventional clinical data into ML-based prognostic models, supporting more individualized risk prediction (47, 48).Machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and gradient boosting methods such as XGBoost, have been applied to predict outcomes in sepsis, COVID-19, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) by integrating clinical and molecular data (47-50). For instance, in targeted metabolomic analyses of patients with CCHF, ML models have been used to analyze amino acid profiles, enabling the prediction of intensive care requirements with high reported accuracy. In parallel, specialized computational frameworks have facilitated biomarker discovery using transcriptomic and metabolomic datasets, expanding opportunities for precision prognostic modeling (50).Despite these encouraging findings, most prognostic models have been developed using retrospective datasets and lack prospective external validation. Challenges related to data imbalance, heterogeneous patient populations, and differences in clinical practice continue to limit model generalizability. Future studies should prioritize multicenter validation, standardized reporting, and assessment of clinical impact to determine whether improved predictive performance translates into better patient outcomes. AI in Scientific Writing and Scholarly PublishingArtificial intelligence is increasingly incorporated into the research and publication process, supporting activities ranging from literature retrieval and evidence synthesis to manuscript preparation and editorial screening. Unlike clinical decision-support applications, these tools primarily aim to improve research efficiency rather than generate new scientific evidence. Their growing adoption has also raised important questions regarding transparency, accountability, and responsible use. AI-powered literature discovery platforms use NLP and citation network analysis to facilitate literature screening, identify relevant publications, and support evidence synthesis (51). full_text_sections.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing healthcare, with growing relevance in infectious diseases and clinical microbiology. This review summarizes current applications of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) in these areas while critically evaluating their strengths and limitations. Although AI has shown promising performance in image analysis, molecular diagnostics, risk prediction, and clinical decision support, its routine implementation remains constrained by limited external validation, heterogeneous datasets, algorithmic bias, and challenges in generalizability and explainability. The review also discusses AI’s emerging role in scientific writing and the ethical and practical considerations associated with its clinical adoption. Overall, current evidence suggests that AI should be regarded as a complementary decision-support technology whose safe and effective integration depends on rigorous validation, high-quality data, and appropriate clinical oversight.
full_text_sections.other: The Dawn of Artificial Intelligence in HealthcareArtificial intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science that develops computational systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence, including pattern recognition, prediction, and decision support. Artificial intelligence has become increasingly integrated into healthcare, offering new opportunities to improve diagnostics, prognostic assessment, and clinical decision-making. Recent advances in machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs), together with the increasing availability of digital health data, have accelerated the development of AI applications across medicine (1).In infectious diseases and clinical microbiology (IDCM), AI has attracted growing interest because it can improve laboratory diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, prognostic assessment, outbreak surveillance, and clinical decision support. Although numerous studies have reported promising results, important challenges related to external validation, data quality, model generalizability, and clinical implementation continue to limit the routine adoption of these technologies.This review was prepared based on the thematic discussions, expert presentations, and literature evaluations conducted within the 2025 Basic Education Program of the Assistants and Young Specialists Commission of the Turkish Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases, entitled AI in Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology. Building on these educational activities, this review critically synthesizes current evidence on AI applications in IDCM, highlighting both their clinical potential and the methodological, practical, and ethical challenges that must be addressed before widespread implementation. The Role of AI in MedicineAI in medicine has evolved from early rule-based expert systems to modern ML and DL models capable of analyzing complex clinical data (2, 3). These approaches have been widely adopted in specialties such as radiology and pathology, where image-based analysis has demonstrated substantial clinical utility (4, 5). In contrast, AI applications in IDCM remain at an earlier stage of implementation because they require integrating microbiological, clinical, and epidemiological information. Accordingly, AI systems in this field should be evaluated according to their specific clinical applications, evidence base, and limitations rather than as a single technology. Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have demonstrated high diagnostic performance in automated Gram stain interpretation and digital culture plate analysis, with reported agreement rates exceeding 95% under controlled experimental conditions (6). Nevertheless, further validation in diverse laboratory settings is required before widespread implementation.Artificial intelligence has also advanced molecular diagnostics through automated analysis of whole-genome sequencing data. title: Determinants of Age‐Appropriate Childhood Immunization Uptake: A Cross‐Sectional Study of Caregiver, Child, Knowledge, Access, and Attitudinal Factors

source_records.title: Determinants of Age‐Appropriate Childhood Immunization Uptake: A Cross‐Sectional Study of Caregiver, Child, Knowledge, Access, and Attitudinal Factors

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: ABSTRACTBackgroundChildhood immunization is among the most cost‐effective public health strategies for reducing under‐five morbidity and mortality. However, full immunization coverage for age remains suboptimal in many low‐ and middle‐income countries due to factors related to caregivers, children, health systems, and sociocultural contexts. The study aimed to assess the prevalence of full immunization for age and identify its associated determinants across multiple domains.MethodsA community‐based cross‐sectional study was conducted among 364 caregiver–child pairs. Full immunization for age was the outcome variable. Data were collected using a structured interviewer‐administered questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, child factors, caregiver knowledge and perceptions, access to health services, and attitudes and practices. Chi‐square tests identified associations, and variables significant at p < 0.05 were entered into multivariable logistic regression models to determine independent predictors.ResultsOverall, 261 children (71.7%) were fully immunized for age. Caregiver education was a strong predictor: children of caregivers with primary (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 3.91), secondary (AOR = 3.30), and tertiary education (AOR = 4.71) were significantly more likely to be fully immunized than those with no education. Rural residence increased the odds of full immunization (AOR = 3.23), as did household size ≥6 (AOR = 2.06). Older child age strongly predicted full immunization, particularly among children aged 12–17 months (AOR = 5.42) and 18–23 months (AOR = 6.83). Health facility delivery nearly quadrupled the likelihood of full immunization (AOR = 3.96). Reliance on non‐health worker information sources reduced uptake, whereas shorter travel time to facilities, regular community immunization sessions, intention for catch‐up vaccination (AOR = 8.74), and positive community advocacy significantly increased coverage.ConclusionFull immunization for age is shaped by caregiver education, child age, health service accessibility, and caregiver attitudes. Interventions should prioritize caregiver education, strengthen health‐worker‐led communication, promote facility‐based deliveries, and expand regular community immunization services to improve coverage.Keywords: caregiver education, child health, childhood immunization, health service access, vaccine uptake Full immunization for age was achieved by 71.7% of children. Caregiver education, health facility delivery, rural residence, regular community immunization services, and positive caregiver attitudes significantly increased coverage, highlighting the need to strengthen primary health care services, health education, and equitable access to routine childhood immunization. 2.Methodology2.1.Study Design and SettingThis study employed a community‐based cross‐sectional design to assess the immunization status of children and identify factors associated with full immunization for age. The study was conducted in 12 selected communities within Nasarawa local government area (LGA) of Nasarawa State, North‐Central Nigeria (Figure 1). Nasarawa LGA is administratively divided into 15 political wards, namely, Udenin Gida, Akum, Udenin, Loko, Tunga/Bakono, Guto/Aisa, Nasarawa North, Nasarawa East, Nasarawa Central, Nasarawa Main Town, Ara I, Ara II, Laminga, Kanah/Ondo/Apawu, and Odu.FIGURE 1Image showing the study location (Nassarawa or Nasarawa State) used for the study in ash color, culled from Aremu et al. 2025 [25].The study communities were selected using a multistage sampling technique. In the first stage, six wards were selected from the 15 wards using simple random sampling (balloting). In the second stage, two communities were randomly selected from each of the selected wards, yielding a total of 12 communities. Eligible households with children aged 12–23 months were subsequently identified using systematic household sampling. This multistage sampling approach ensured that communities from different geographical areas of the LGA were represented while minimizing selection bias.Nasarawa LGA is served by a network of public and private health facilities that provide routine immunization services in accordance with Nigeria's National Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI). These services target children from birth to 23 months of age and include vaccines against tuberculosis, poliomyelitis, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcal disease, rotavirus, measles, yellow fever, meningitis A, and other nationally recommended antigens according to the Nigerian National Immunization Schedule.Routine immunization services in the study area are delivered through fixed sessions at health facilities and periodic community outreach activities, particularly in hard‐to‐reach and underserved settlements. These outreach services are coordinated by the Nasarawa Local Government Primary Health Care Authority in collaboration with the Nasarawa State Primary Health Care Development Agency and the National Primary Health Care Development Agency to improve geographical access and equity in vaccine delivery. The community‐based design enabled the inclusion of both users and nonusers of routine immunization services, thereby providing a more representative assessment of childhood immunization coverage and its associated determinants within the LGA.2.2.Study PopulationThe study population consisted of caregivers of children aged 0–23 months residing in the study area at the time of the survey. A caregiver was defined as any adult, most commonly the mother, who was primarily responsible for the child's day‐to‐day care and immunization decisions. Caregivers who had lived in the community for at least 6 months prior to the study were eligible to participate. Caregivers who were severely ill or unwilling to provide informed consent at the time of data collection were excluded.2.3.Sample Size Determination and Sampling TechniqueThe sample size was determined using the Cochran single population proportion formula for estimating proportions in large populations: n=Z2×p×1−pd2where n is the required minimum sample size. full_text_sections.abstract: ABSTRACTBackgroundChildhood immunization is among the most cost‐effective public health strategies for reducing under‐five morbidity and mortality. However, full immunization coverage for age remains suboptimal in many low‐ and middle‐income countries due to factors related to caregivers, children, health systems, and sociocultural contexts. The study aimed to assess the prevalence of full immunization for age and identify its associated determinants across multiple domains.MethodsA community‐based cross‐sectional study was conducted among 364 caregiver–child pairs. Full immunization for age was the outcome variable. Data were collected using a structured interviewer‐administered questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, child factors, caregiver knowledge and perceptions, access to health services, and attitudes and practices. Chi‐square tests identified associations, and variables significant at p < 0.05 were entered into multivariable logistic regression models to determine independent predictors.ResultsOverall, 261 children (71.7%) were fully immunized for age. Caregiver education was a strong predictor: children of caregivers with primary (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 3.91), secondary (AOR = 3.30), and tertiary education (AOR = 4.71) were significantly more likely to be fully immunized than those with no education. Rural residence increased the odds of full immunization (AOR = 3.23), as did household size ≥6 (AOR = 2.06). Older child age strongly predicted full immunization, particularly among children aged 12–17 months (AOR = 5.42) and 18–23 months (AOR = 6.83). Health facility delivery nearly quadrupled the likelihood of full immunization (AOR = 3.96). Reliance on non‐health worker information sources reduced uptake, whereas shorter travel time to facilities, regular community immunization sessions, intention for catch‐up vaccination (AOR = 8.74), and positive community advocacy significantly increased coverage.ConclusionFull immunization for age is shaped by caregiver education, child age, health service accessibility, and caregiver attitudes. Interventions should prioritize caregiver education, strengthen health‐worker‐led communication, promote facility‐based deliveries, and expand regular community immunization services to improve coverage.Keywords: caregiver education, child health, childhood immunization, health service access, vaccine uptake Full immunization for age was achieved by 71.7% of children. Caregiver education, health facility delivery, rural residence, regular community immunization services, and positive caregiver attitudes significantly increased coverage, highlighting the need to strengthen primary health care services, health education, and equitable access to routine childhood immunization.

full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionThis study provides comprehensive evidence on the multifactorial determinants of age‐appropriate childhood immunization, integrating caregiver sociodemographic characteristics, child‐related factors, knowledge and perceptions, access to health services, and attitudes and practices. In general, nearly three‐quarters of children were fully immunized for age, a coverage level that, while encouraging, still falls short of global and national targets required to achieve herd immunity against vaccine‐preventable diseases [26, 27, 28]. The findings underscore that immunization uptake is shaped not by a single factor but by intersecting individual, household, community, and health system influences.Caregiver education emerged as one of the strongest and most consistent predictors of full immunization for age. Children whose caregivers had primary, secondary, or tertiary education were between three and five times more likely to be fully immunized compared with those whose caregivers had no formal education. This gradient effect suggests a dose–response relationship between educational attainment and immunization behavior, reinforcing evidence from multiple low‐ and middle‐income country settings [7]. Education likely enhances health literacy, improves comprehension of immunization schedules, and increases caregivers’ confidence in interacting with health services [7, 8, 9, 10]. Importantly, the magnitude of association observed in this study indicates that even basic education confers substantial benefits for child health, highlighting the broader intersectoral value of investments in female and caregiver education [17, 29, 30].An unexpected but notable finding was the higher likelihood of full immunization among children residing in rural areas compared with urban residents. This contrasts with much of the existing literature, where urban residence is often associated with better immunization outcomes due to proximity to health facilities [31, 32, 33, 34]. However, this finding may reflect the effectiveness of targeted rural outreach services, community‐based immunization sessions, and stronger social cohesion in rural settings, which can facilitate information sharing and collective health‐seeking behaviors. Conversely, urban settings, particularly informal settlements, may face challenges such as population mobility, competing livelihood demands, and weaker continuity of care. This result emphasizes the need to disaggregate “urban” contexts and address urban inequities rather than assuming universal advantage.Household size was also independently associated with immunization status, with children from households of six or more members being more likely to be fully immunized. Larger households may benefit from shared caregiving responsibilities, prior experience with immunization among older siblings, and accumulated knowledge of health services [35, 36, 37, 38]. This finding contrasts with studies reporting reduced immunization uptake in larger households due to resource constraints, suggesting that contextual factors, such as social support networks, may modify the effect of household size.Child‐related factors showed strong associations with immunization status. Increasing child age was a powerful predictor of full immunization, with children aged 12–23 months having five‐ to sevenfold higher odds of being fully immunized compared with infants aged 0–5 months [39, 40]. This pattern reflects the cumulative nature of immunization schedules and highlights missed opportunities for timely vaccination in early infancy. Health facility delivery was another critical determinant, nearly quadrupling the likelihood of full immunization. Facility‐based delivery provides early contact with health workers, immediate initiation of vaccines, issuance of immunization cards, and counseling of caregivers, thereby establishing a continuum of care that extends into routine immunization.Caregiver knowledge and information sources played a pivotal role in shaping immunization outcomes [40, 41, 42, 43, 44]. Although general awareness of immunization was high, the source of information significantly influenced uptake. Children whose caregivers relied on family, friends, or religious leaders for immunization information were substantially less likely to be fully immunized than those informed by health workers. This finding highlights the central role of trusted, technically competent health workers in countering misinformation and building vaccine confidence [41, 42]. It also underscores the potential risk posed by informal information channels if they are not aligned with evidence‐based messages.Access‐related factors further illuminated structural barriers to immunization. Shorter travel time to immunization sites and the availability of regular community immunization sessions significantly increased the likelihood of full immunization. These findings align with health systems research emphasizing convenience, proximity, and service reliability as key drivers of service utilization [26]. Notably, children who had ever missed an immunization were dramatically less likely to be fully immunized, illustrating how early disruptions in vaccination schedules can have lasting consequences. This underscores the importance of reminder systems, defaulter tracking, and flexible catch‐up strategies.Attitudes and practices were among the most powerful predictors observed in this study. Caregivers who intended to seek catch‐up immunization after missed doses had almost ninefold higher odds of having fully immunized children, whereas willingness to recommend immunization to others also significantly increased uptake. These findings suggest that positive normative beliefs and proactive health‐seeking intentions are critical levers for improving immunization coverage [45, 46, 47]. Conversely, decision‐making dominated by extended family members or community leaders was associated with reduced likelihood of full immunization, reflecting the complex influence of social hierarchies and cultural norms on health behaviors [18].Taken together, these findings have important implications for policy and practice. Interventions to improve childhood immunization should adopt a multidimensional approach that strengthens caregiver education and health literacy, reinforces health‐worker‐led communication, promotes facility‐based deliveries, and expands regular, community‐based immunization services. Engaging influential community figures with accurate, context‐sensitive information may help transform them from barriers into facilitators of immunization. Addressing early missed vaccinations through robust follow‐up and catch‐up strategies is particularly critical for sustaining full immunization coverage.4.1.Strengths and Limitations of the StudyA key strength of this study lies in its comprehensive analytical approach, which examined childhood immunization determinants across multiple domains, including caregiver sociodemographic characteristics, child‐related factors, knowledge and perceptions, access to health services, and caregiver attitudes and practices. This multidimensional framework provides a nuanced understanding of the complex pathways influencing age‐appropriate immunization and enhances the relevance of the findings for policy and programmatic decision‐making. The use of multivariable logistic regression allowed for adjustment of potential confounders, strengthening the internal validity of the identified associations. In addition, verification of immunization status using vaccination cards, where available, improved data accuracy and reduced misclassification bias.Despite these strengths, several limitations should be acknowledged. The cross‐sectional design precludes causal inference, as exposure and outcome were assessed simultaneously. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionThis study demonstrates that full, age‐appropriate childhood immunization is shaped by a complex interplay of caregiver characteristics, child‐related factors, health system accessibility, and social and behavioral influences. Caregiver education emerged as a particularly strong determinant, underscoring the critical role of health literacy in promoting timely and complete vaccination. Child age and place of delivery further highlighted the importance of early and continuous engagement with health services, especially through facility‐based deliveries that facilitate linkage to routine immunization. Access‐related factors, including travel time to immunization sites and the availability of regular community immunization sessions, significantly influenced uptake, emphasizing the need for convenient and reliable service delivery. Attitudes and practices, such as intention for catch‐up immunization, peer recommendation, and decision‐making autonomy, were among the most powerful predictors of full immunization, revealing the central role of caregiver motivation and social influence. To achieve and sustain high immunization coverage, interventions must go beyond vaccine availability to address educational, behavioral, and structural barriers simultaneously. Strengthening health‐worker‐led communication, promoting community‐based immunization strategies, and supporting caregivers to complete missed doses are essential for closing persistent coverage gaps. An integrated, people‐centered approach is, therefore, critical to advancing equitable childhood immunization and improving child survival outcomes.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionImmunization is universally recognized as one of the most effective and economical public health interventions for preventing infectious diseases and reducing childhood morbidity and mortality [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Vaccines avert estimated millions of deaths globally each year and contribute significantly to improved child survival, cognitive development, and long‐term population health outcomes [2, 3]. Despite these benefits, many countries continue to experience suboptimal immunization coverage, particularly with respect to children being fully immunized for age according to national and World Health Organization (WHO) schedules [6, 7].In low‐ and middle‐income countries, gaps in routine immunization persist due to a combination of demand‐side and supply‐side factors [7]. These include caregiver‐related characteristics such as education, knowledge, beliefs, and decision‐making autonomy; child‐related factors such as age and place of delivery; and health system factors, including accessibility, quality of services, and reliability of vaccine supply [8, 9, 10]. Sociocultural norms and community‐level influences further shape caregivers’ perceptions and practices regarding childhood vaccination [11, 12, 13, 14, 15].Caregiver education has consistently emerged as a strong predictor of childhood immunization uptake [11, 16]. Educated caregivers are more likely to understand the purpose and schedule of vaccines, recognize the risks of vaccine‐preventable diseases, and navigate health services effectively [17]. Conversely, limited education may exacerbate misinformation, fear of adverse events, and reliance on informal information sources such as family members or religious leaders, which may undermine confidence in vaccines [16, 17, 18]. The role of information sources is, therefore, critical, as health workers are often the most trusted and accurate conveyors of immunization‐related information [19, 20].Child‐specific factors also play a crucial role in immunization status. Age is particularly important, as younger children may not yet be eligible for all scheduled vaccines, whereas missed opportunities early in life can lead to incomplete immunization later [21, 22]. Place of delivery has been shown to influence early initiation and continuity of immunization, with health facility deliveries facilitating immediate linkage to routine immunization services, provision of vaccination cards, and caregiver counseling [23, 24].Access to health services remains a major determinant of immunization uptake [10, 11, 12]. Physical distance to health facilities, transportation challenges, travel time, and the availability of regular outreach or community‐based immunization sessions all affect caregivers’ ability to complete vaccination schedules [16, 25]. Even where vaccines are provided free of charge, indirect costs such as transportation and opportunity costs related to time away from work may discourage caregivers from attending immunization sessions [9, 10, 11]. Health system factors, such as long waiting times, perceived disrespect from health workers, and vaccine stock‐outs, can further erode trust and reduce utilization of services.Beyond knowledge and access, caregiver attitudes and practices significantly shape immunization behaviors [10]. Intentions to seek catch‐up immunization after missed doses, willingness to recommend immunization to others, and the influence of key decision‐makers within households and communities are powerful drivers of vaccine uptake. In many settings, immunization decisions are not made solely by mothers but are influenced by spouses, extended family members, community leaders, and religious authorities [12]. Understanding these dynamics is essential for designing culturally sensitive and community‐responsive interventions.Given the multifaceted nature of immunization determinants, there is a need for comprehensive analyses that simultaneously examine sociodemographic, child‐related, knowledge‐based, access‐related, and attitudinal factors. This study therefore aimed to assess the prevalence of full immunization for age and identify its associated determinants across multiple domains. Evidence generated from this study is intended to inform targeted strategies to strengthen routine immunization programs, enhance caregiver engagement, and ultimately improve child health outcomes. 2.2.Study PopulationThe study population consisted of caregivers of children aged 0–23 months residing in the study area at the time of the survey. A caregiver was defined as any adult, most commonly the mother, who was primarily responsible for the child's day‐to‐day care and immunization decisions. Caregivers who had lived in the community for at least 6 months prior to the study were eligible to participate. Caregivers who were severely ill or unwilling to provide informed consent at the time of data collection were excluded. 2.3.Sample Size Determination and Sampling TechniqueThe sample size was determined using the Cochran single population proportion formula for estimating proportions in large populations: n=Z2×p×1−pd2where n is the required minimum sample size. Z is the standard normal deviate corresponding to a 95% confidence level (1.96). p is the estimated prevalence of full immunization from previous similar studies. d is the margin of error (precision), set at 5% (0.05).Assuming an estimated prevalence (p) of full immunization of 0.50, a conservative estimate commonly used when population prevalence varies across settings to maximize sample size, the initial sample size was calculated as follows: n=(1.96)2×0.50×(1−0.50)(0.05)2n=3.84×0.250.0025n=384To account for potential nonresponse or incomplete data, an adjustment of approximately 5% was applied: nadjusted=384×(1−0.05)≈364Thus, a minimum sample size of 364 caregiver–child pairs was deemed sufficient to ensure adequate statistical power and precision for estimating the proportion of fully immunized children.A multistage sampling technique was used to select participants. In the first stage, communities were selected using simple random sampling. In the second stage, households with eligible children aged 0–23 months were identified through household listing. Where more than one eligible child was present in a household, one child was selected by simple random sampling. The corresponding caregiver of the selected child was then interviewed. 2.4.Data Collection Instrument and ProcedureData were collected using a structured interviewer‐administered questionnaire developed on the basis of relevant literature and national immunization guidelines. The questionnaire comprised five sections: sociodemographic characteristics of caregivers and households; child‐related factors; caregiver knowledge and perceptions regarding immunization; access to health services and perceived barriers; and caregiver attitudes and practices toward childhood immunization.Immunization status was verified primarily through review of the child's immunization card. In cases where the card was unavailable, caregiver recall was used as a supplementary source of information. Data collection was conducted by trained research assistants who were fluent in the local language and familiar with the study context. The questionnaire was pretested in a community outside the study area, and necessary adjustments were made to improve clarity and consistency. 2.5.Study Variables and Operational DefinitionsThe dependent variable was child immunization status, categorized as fully immunized for age or not fully immunized for age. Introduction For more than 1000 days, the armed conflict that began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has profoundly disrupted health care nationally. Between April 2023 and June 2024, an estimated 26 000 deaths occurred in Khartoum State alone due to intentional injury-related causes, indicating the high levels of brutality in this densely populated area (1). There have been reports of physical injuries and disabilities with mental health consequences, in addition to rape and other forms of sexual violence, with approximately 6.9 million women and girls, and an increasing number of men and boys, at risk of gender- based violence (GBV) (2). The prolonged siege has triggered acute food insecurity and mass displacement has placed severe strains on livelihoods and deepened financial insecurity (2). The high levels of malnutrition, frequent disease outbreaks and worsening outcomes for individuals living with chronic conditions have resulted in increased morbidity and mortality. Maternal and neonatal deaths have increased markedly, alongside the increasing threat of antimicrobial resistance (2). Sudan’s health system is experiencing extreme dysfunction. Within 6 months from the onset of the war, nearly two-thirds of hospitals and medical centres had ceased operations (3). Looting of health facilities and medical supply stores has disrupted service delivery and created a critical shortage of essential medicines. These issues are further exacerbated by violence against health workers and a severe workforce shortage (3). Consequently, disease surveillance and health service delivery coordination have been significantly disrupted, with significant deterioration in availability, accessibility and quality of health care service nationwide (2,3). This commentary adds to existing evidence by highlighting the current state of Sudan’s health system amidst ongoing conflict, including its implications for the region, the urgency of required intervention, and actionable recommendations for the Sudanese Ministry of Health, World Health Organization and other partners. Health system collapse In conflict-affected areas, health facilities are compelled to shut down as a result of multiple intersecting factors, including persistent insecurity, looting, damage of medical infrastructure, severe shortage of health personnel, and difficulties in obtaining essential medical supplies (4). For example, in war-affected regions where ambulances are looted, communities are forced to rely on donkey carts and wheelbarrows as improvised means of transporting patients. Sudan’s pharmaceutical sector has largely ceased production of essential medicines, including antibiotics and established pharmaceutical distribution networks have been seriously disrupted, resulting in medication shortage and increased costs for pharmacies and patients (5). Targeted damage to telecommunications and health information infrastructure, together with attacks on health workers, has severely undermined the country’s health information systems. These deliberate disruptions have significantly impacted the ability to collect and transmit data, affecting the development of essential health system baseline data (4). In addition to injuries caused by the conflict, Sudan is witnessing extensive cases of infections, which are causing a health crisis. Cholera, malaria, measles, polio, and dengue fever infections have increased markedly, with more than 120 000 confirmed cholera cases alone responsible for more than 3000 deaths (6). Humanitarian efforts to address these constraints have achieved limited success, partly due to the shortage of personnel in coordination roles and insufficient presence at the state level. These challenges, compounded by inadequate funding and limited political pressure on the warring parties to comply with international humanitarian law and permit access, have resulted in the humanitarian response reaching only a small fraction of those in need (7). Implications for the region Sudan’s war has triggered the largest displacement crisis worldwide, with more than 14.5 million displaced— over 10.5 million inside the country and approximately 594 Commentary EMHJ – Vol. 32 No. 9 – 2026 4 million across borders into neighbouring countries, including Central African Republic, Chad, Egypt, Ethiopia, Libya, and South Sudan (8). As of September 2023, Chad alone had received more than 420 000 refugees, with crude mortality rates up to 20 times higher than before the conflict, due mainly to violence (9). These massive movements of people are placing overwhelming pressure on fragile health systems across the region. The effects on public health are not limited to Sudan; border-crossing by refugees has increased the risk of infectious disease transmission. The malaria, cholera and measles outbreaks have been fuelled by overcrowded camps with poor sanitation, interrupted vaccination programmes and limited medical services (10). As of March 2025, only 14% of hospitals and 16% of primary care facilities were still operating in Sudan, due to the worst conflict-driven humanitarian crisis in the world (11). The country's capacity to identify, stop and handle epidemics has been seriously compromised. These regional realities underscore the urgent need for coordinated cross-border health strategies. International cooperation is required to improve camp conditions, resume immunisation programmes, restore health care, and strengthen cross-border disease surveillance (10). Sudan’s unfolding health emergency is no longer confined within its boundaries; without collective action, it will continue to reverberate across the region, jeopardizing disease control and stretching humanitarian systems in multiple countries (9). Urgent priorities The destruction of infrastructure, mass displacement and increasing disease burdens are causing preventable morbidity and mortality. There is an urgent need to scale- up humanitarian assistance (4). Immediate priorities include maintaining access to health services using multiple approaches such as the use of mobile clinics, rebuilding health facilities at all levels of care, ensuring the protection of health care from attacks, and providing logistic support to guarantee a continuous flow of medical supplies (13). Sustained funding and operational support, alongside community empowerment and support to locally led initiatives (13), are critical to preserve life- saving capacity for immediate relief and long-term health system resilience. Supporting public health campaigns and community-based health promotions, including among displaced populations, could prevent disease outbreaks while improving access to available health care services (11). Expanding the cross-border health corridors would make services accessible to populations that have become inaccessible due to displacement, particularly along the borders with South Sudan and Chad, where the collapse of surveillance and referral networks have disrupted care and made people more susceptible to epidemics (11). WHO-led regional coordination efforts, in cooperation with relevant ministries of health, may facilitate the establishment of common surveillance channels, mobilisation of emergency response teams and coordination of health services where domestic efforts have failed. For example, opening the Adre Border crossing between Chad and Sudan is considered essential to enable the delivery of lifesaving humanitarian assistance (14). Evidence-based, effective and sustainable interven­ tions in conflict-affected settings in Ethiopia, Lebanon, South Africa, and Syria have shown that effective health response in conflict settings are dependent on strong governance, community involvement, capacity building, and integrated multisectoral strategies (4). Humanitarian and development organizations, in collaboration with the WHO, should support capacity-building of local authori­ ties and strengthening of local governance. The Ministry of Health and local actors should be supported to lead and help coordinate response, ensuring stronger local capac­ ity for recovery. To improve outbreaks control the Ministry of Health, with technical and logistics support from WHO and partners, should deploy rapid response teams to help restore surveillance and early warning systems, and stabilise supply chains, and support security for health workers. Donor-enabled interventions should extend beyond emergency aid to ensuring that the crisis does not evolve into a broader regional public health emergency (13). Conclusion Sudan is facing a severe humanitarian crisis characterised by conflict, displacement, mass casualties, and multiple disease outbreaks, compounded by the crippling of the health system. There is an urgent need to scale-up humanitarian efforts to improve access to health services at all levels and across care cascades, including curative and community-based preventive services, to ensure the delivery of immediate relief and increase resilience of the health system.
